speechtext: That all rules and orders he suspended in relation to a Bill to amend the Act of the. present session intituled 1 An Act to incorporate the Thorold and Lake Erie Railway Comlpiainy-'
Explain.

Unfortunately clerical errors occurred in the Bill. The names of Mr. HAGGART.
three of the incorporators :	Mr. Noreross,

It is simply sought to amend clerical errors. There is a precedent for this procedure. In the journals of the House of Commons of 1887, in the motion, of Mr. Kirkpatrick seconded by Mr. Hesson, a similar motion was made with regard to the Kincardine and Teeswater Railway Company. The Bill was presented to the House, received and read the first time ; a resolution was passed authorizing the second and third readings, and it was then ordered that the clerk should carry the Bill to the Senate and desire their concurrence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I suppose my hon. friend is entitled to have the Bill read the first time, but I do not think the rules of the House should be suspended to a greater extent than that. I presume the facts are just as stated, and that this is simply to correct clerical errors, but as it is a private Bill and there may be interested parties, I think it would be unwise to suspend all rules at once and to say that the Bill should be carried through without further investigation. I would suggest that the Bill should be read the first time, and referred to the Committee on Standing Orders where it can be examined.

Motion agreed to, and Bill introduced and read the first time.

The House will observe that there'is an additional vote asked for of $4,000. This is principally by reason of the appointment of an accountant, who is a new

officer, at $1,800. Two officers were transferred from the ordinary charge for clerical assistance and put on the permanent list, making $1,000. The remainder is for statutory increases. The appointment of an accountant was rendered necessary by the fact that very large sums are now being disbursed through the department for bounties and other purposes.
Who has been appointed accountant ?	;

Code. He was formerly assistant in the Customs Department, and has been transferred to mine.
Mr. BLA1N. How long has Mr. Code been in the employ of the government ?
About twenty years.
Will the bon. gentleman mention in what cases the statutory increases occur?	,
A chief clerk, $50; a first-class clerk, $50; a second-class clerk, $50; five junior second-class clerks, $50 each; three third-class clerks and two messengers.
Will the hon. minister explain to the committee that well-known phrase which we see so frequently now in the estimates: 'notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act ? '

That refers to the case of the accountant. He was in the service of the Customs Department as assistant accountant at $1,600. On being transferred to this department, where the service required from him is more responsible and more important, his salary has [DOT]been raised to' $1,800.
Have all the clerks in the hon. gentleman's department who were entitled to the statutory increase received that increase?

Yes.
Mr. 'LENNOX. I would like . the hon. gentleman to inform the committee whether in the reorganization of the department the hon. gentleman has pursued the course laid down in the statute. I would also call the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact of there being now two messengers instead of one.
There have always been two messengers, only one has heretofore been paid out of the contingencies instead of out of the main vote.

The hon. gentleman has not stated whether the statute has been complied with in the re-organization of the Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
department. It is somewhat surprising to find an increase in this department of even $4,000, in view of the record of the right hon. gentleman at the head of that depart-Kinent as a public man, and in view of his explicit statement made on several occasions that it was a useless department orij which the expenditure of public money could not be justified.

The major item is the increase for the accountant. That is due to the very large expenditures now paid through the department on bounties and mail subsidies. The $1,000 increase in the mail clerks has been caused by a transfer. It was formerly paid from contingencies and is now paid directly. The rest are all statutory increases. Touching the work of the department, it may interest the hon. gentleman to know that, if the correspondence is any guide, it has increased just 600 per cent within the last six or seven years. There is a great deal more done than in 1896. There are six times as many letters and almost six times as much work in other ways.
You have fifteen clerks instead of ten.
Three are mere transfers. The only new appointment is the accountant.
The right hon. gentleman has not answered my question as to the manner in which this alteration is made in the department.

The chief alteration was the appointment of a new accountant. The only other material alteration was in handing over the commercial agencies to the assistant Deputy Minister for special control. The rest is as before.

-We have this fact established at any rate. The right hon. gentleman was wanting to say that this was a useless department and the money spent on it was wasted. Yet we are now asked to vote $31,800 on that department, including the salary of the minister. That is a large amount for the country to have to pay for a department which the right hon. gentleman has often declared is absolutely unnecessary and useless.
But there is an alteration between 1896 and 1904.
Yes, there is another occupant of the position,.

The Civil Service Act stipulates that in order to effect a change in the organization of a department, such as is asked for here, certain steps have to be taken. There must be a recommendation from the deputy head to the head of the department, that recommendation must be

concurred in by the head of the department, and then laid before the Council. That procedure has, however, been neglected by the various departments.

In all
cases where there has been any new creation, a report of the deputy head has always been obtained. I have here a memo, from Mr. McGee, showing the practice prior to 1896. In several cases the reports of the deputy heads were presented to parliament and in almost all the others the appointments were made after parliament prorogued. I shall send my hon. friend the memorandum.

The question is not the qualifications of an official, but the creation of the office, so that the fact that the accountant was in another department is not material. The statute provides, wisely or otherwise, that before this is done a certain course shall be pursued and among other things that the promotions or introduction of a new clerkship shall be upon
the recommendation of the deputy head setting forth in writing the reasons why he makes the suggestion or recommendation.
I am not arguing the question in the legal sense, but am speaking of it only as a matter of propriety in carrying out the provisions-of the statute.
' Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT. As a matter of course an Order in Council was passed authorizing this appointment.

What I object to is that: there has not been a recommendation inwriting by the head of the department as an initial step in the proceedings.
Civil government, contingencies, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act*. $6,600.

There-is a reduction here of about.$100 in all. In, 1903 the vote for clerical and other assistance was $2,500. That is now reduced to L500-. Two sections were made of this, part of it being transferred to the main estimates. Under printing and stationery we ask $2,000 in 1903-4 and $2,300 now. My deputy informs me that the increase is on account of the various bounties required. There is a saving in the case of sundries which were $2,500 and are now $2,300. The total asked in 1903 was $7,000, the total asked now is $6,600.
Ocean and mail service between Great Britain and Canada, $260,000.
What do they now receive for the ' Bavarian ' and ' Tunisian ? '
They are to have an effectual actual speed of 17 knots.
What is the speed of the ' Tunisian ' and ' Bavarian ? '
It is supposed to be about 14i to 15 knots. They seem to have kept that speed this year and a good deal better than in former times. Of late they have been doing a good deal better than last year.
For what reason was the increased subsidy given ?

I cut down their demands in the matter of the new steamers very considerably, and allowed them a little more in the case of the ' Bavarian ' and ' Tunisian.' It was a kind of lumping business for the whole service. They complained that they lost money on the trips. Whether that is so or not I cannot say, but I made large reductions from the amounts they demanded for the new steamers and gave a slight increase for the ' Bavarian ' and ' Tunisian.'
Provided always they live up to their contract. There is a special clause under which, if they fail, they are fined one per cent for each hour.
Has that fine ever been collected ?
I cannot enforce it in their case because the steamers have not yet been put on the service.
Has it been collected in any ease ?
Oh, yes, I have several times imposed fines for failure to live up to the time stipulated in the contract.
Where will I find the particulars ? Does the bon. gentleman remember how much the deductions have amounted to ?

For failing to make the time ? What was the average time made Mr. CLARKE.
for the last twelve months and how does it compare with the time made during the previous twelve months.
During the summer of 1903 they appear to have made 30 trips at an average time of 7 days 12 .hours and 47 minutes, that is fron Mo-ville to Rimouski.
What does that mean in knots per hour ?
All depends on whether they went south or through the Belle Isle passage.

The hon. gentleman must have the figures before him. I would like to know what is the average speed per hour, and the hon. gentleman says that depends on whether they took one passage or the other. Of course, he has the distances by both routes before him ?

From Rimouski to Moville, via Belle Isle, 2,287 knots ; and from Rimouski to Moville by Cape Race, the shortest possible route, 2,445 knots. That amounts to 7 days 12 hours and 47 minutes. With respect to Cape Race, that is probably shorter than the true time, because they are compelled to go further south in passing by Cape Race.
What is the tonnage of these steamers ?
Would the minister state what arrangements have been made under this contract during the winter months for the St. Lawrence navigation ?

In the winter months they sail from St. John and Halifax, and a little longer time is allowed in winter-I think 12 hours additional time for the same steamers. The contract stipulates that in each case of these new steamers, the ' Bavarian ' and the ' Tunisian,' ten full round trips must be made. The hon. gentleman will understand that all these steamers have to be taken off for a certain time for ordinary repair, and this is done during the winter.
The old Beaver Line is not under contract now ?

No ; our only contract for this service is with the Allans. This contract is expected to run two years.
Mr. iSPROULE. In making a new contract like that it is a great pity that some arrangements have not been made for a faster service. I understood the minister to say that the new steamers would make about 17 knots an hour. That appears to be very slow compared with the speed that steamiers make between Niew York and

Europe. We appear to be either wasting our time in some way, or to be unequal to the occasion in failing to provide a better service than we have. I think the country will conclude that there is something wrong when we cannot succeed in getting a faster service than the 17 knots an hour that the new steamers are to make. Surely we could provide a greater speed than that.

My hon. friend will note that there are two serious questions to consider. One is the enormously increased expense that an *additional speed would entail. The other arises from the fact that fast steamers can carry only a small amouilt of freight. The amount, I believe, that is carried on a fast steamer is something like 1,400 or 1,500 tons in vessels of 10,000 tonnage or more ; whereas, as he knows, other vessels carry a very heavy freight. I think I have mentioned to the House that we tried to ascertain what could be done for a faster serv Ice. but the only tenders submitted to us called for $1,000,000 in one case, and $1,250,000 in the other, for a 20-knot service, and they appended to it divers conditions which it was not in the power of the government to comply with.
As a matter of fact, taking the mean speed of last year, we have been paying these subsidies for a mean speed of 13 knots per hour. That is the best we have been able to do yet.
Yes.

If I have made the calculation rightly, for the longer passage of 2,455 miles, with a mean time of 7 days and 12 hours, the rate would be 13'6 knots per hour and for the shorter passage of 2.287 miles, 12-7 knots per hour. The average speed, taking both routes into consideration, during the past year, has been 13 knots per hour for the carriage of our mails. Surely we should be able to accelerate that speed in the near future.
knots, taking into account the shorter passage that we have, amounts to almost nothing as between the New York passage and the passage from Moville to Rimouski. 1 may also point out that the average speed is a good deal reduced by- the fact that if vessels like the ' Parisian ' and ' Pretorian ' were employed as subsidiary boats, as well as the ' Bavarian ' and 4 Tunisian,' we would attain a much better average speed than we are attaining with the 4 Bavarian ' and the 4 Tunisian ' as the principal boats. Now, 1 find that the 4 Tunisian ' for the most part did the service in about six and a half days. In July the average was 6 days 21 hours ; August, 6 days 8 hours ; the next time, o davs 9 hours. And in the fall, of course, wlien they had more difficulty with fog and sometimes with ice, the time was done to 7 days 8 hours. But, for the most part, the 4 Bavarian ' and 4 Tunisian ' did the Passage in considerably under 7 days. The distances I gave the hon. gentleman are the shortest possible distances. But in passing along Newfoundland they frequently have to diverge considerably to the ssouth, which lengthens the passage. I may mention also that I have felt rather doubtful whether I ought to insist too rigorously on Ane terms of the contract where they pleaded that the had to stop on account of fog. If you insist too much upon it, you may tempt	Pe '
pie to run at an increased rate of speed under circumstances which may impeU1 safety of the passengers. Therefore, uher_ they'have been detained by fog and ice. I have dealt rather leniently with loss o. time.

What is the intended tonnage of these two new turbine steamers, and is it intended that they are to come up to Montreal ? And I may say to my right hon. friend (Sir Richard Cartwright) that our friends about me here have suggested that he should not give himself the trouble to rise to answer each question that is put to him.

The question is one which has engaged a good deal of attention. I would just point out to my hon. friend that by the terms of the contract which I have made with the Allans, if they are complied with, we will have a service from Moville to Rimouski almost identical in point of time with the New York service. It will take six days with 17-knot steamers. With the exception of one or two of the 4 greyhounds,' the time to New Y'ork is about six days. Now, it is a matter for serious consideration whether it is worth going to an increased expenditure, varying from three-quarters of a million to-a million and a quarter, for the sake of shortening the time by 14 or 15 hours. I leave my hon. friend to consider that question. But I want to point out to him tha* the difference between 17 knots and 20 I

I am much obliged for the hon. gentleman's consideration, and, if I find myself tired, I will retain my seat. With respect to the points mentioned by the hon. gentleman, I may say that I believe that the tonnage of these vessels is to be from S,000 to 10,000 tons. My deputy thinks they will be 10,000 tons. They are the turbines, which, as hon. gentlemen are aware, is a form now coming into considerable favour.
Does not the coutract provide what tonnage they shall be ?
Not specifically as to tonnage, but it provides for their effective speed, and that is about the least tonnage they can have to give that speed.
I did not understand the right hon. gentleman to say whether it is intended that they should come up to Montreal.
Yes, so I understood from the Messrs. Allan.
Does the right hon. gentleman know whether there is any provision for cold storage accommodation ?
Yes, that is expressly provided for.
If I have taken the right hon. gentleman's figures correctly, the average speed of the ' Bavarian ' and ' Tunisian ' last year was not more than fourteen knots ?
No, I do not think it was.
I have tried every possible means but I cannot induce the steamship owners to tender on better terms.

The situation will be this, as the right hon. gentleman knows is the case, unhappily, at the present time-that, while we are subsidizing vessels to carry the Canadian mails, the overwhelming bulk of our mails is being taken to New York and sent thence in British or foreign bottoms.

But my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) will note that there is a steamer going out of New York every day. Under these circumstances it is impossible for us to provide for more than a fraction of our own correspondence. More->
over, from points west of Kingston, the mails would naturally go by New York as being the shorter route. From Kingston eastward our correspondence, including the correspondence of Montreal and the maritime provinces, will go by the Canadian route.	[DOT]
There have been, as the right hon. gentleman knows, repeated memorials addressed to the government favouring the establishment of what may be fairly called a fast Atlantic line.
That is true, and as the hon. gentleman knows we have advertised and tried in every way to obtain terms for such a service. But" the figures have been extremely high.
We went so far on one occasion as to secure the model of a new

style of ship which, it was supposed, would revolutionize Atlantic travel. But that result does not seem to have been attained. But the right hon. gentleman will not say that 15 knots an hour is what is desired by the commercial bodies of this country, and he knows that our passenger traffic is being disintegrated because we have no vessels comparing in luxury and comfort with many of the steamships sailing from New York.
I think my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) will tell the hon. gentleman that the ' Bavarian ' and ' Tunisian ' are great favourites with the travelling public.
With the people of Montreal-they have to go by that route.

No, they could go by New York. But in the summer these boats are well filled. As to the speed, I have made many inquiries, and I find that there are only a very small number of persons who are willing to pay considerably for the increased speed of 20 knots as against 17 knots. The hon. gentleman knows that all you gain by a 20-knot vessel would be fifteen hours in the transit between Moville and Rimouski. He can satisfy himself by making the calculation. It is a serious question whether it is worth while for the people of Canada to pay three-quarters of a million or a million more than we are paying now in order to shorten the passage by fifteen hours, particularly when we shall have to use vessels that will carry extremely little freight.
There is an increase of ,f!85,000 in the vote, yet the mails will go practically as they have been going.

That is true, but we get a very much better service than before. If we get these vessels to make the passage in six days between Moville and Rimouski on the average it will go far to give us the service the hon. gentleman desires. We find, on examination, that the vessels running from New York at the rate of 17 knots are very extensively patronized in comparison with the ' Lucania ' and vessels of that class. The latter vessels, such as the ' Cedric,' I believe, are designed for 17 knots and not for an excessive speed. The cost of increased speed is enormous. Perhaps the hon. gentleman has not examined that point, but if he has examined it he will know that every additional knot involves huge increased expenses.

To have a six-day passage from Rimouski to Moville, it would be necessary to obtain 10 knots on the average. It is not contemplated by the right hon. gentleman, however, that this service is to give much more than 14 knots.

I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) is a little

underrating the speed of tbe ' Bavarian ' and the ' Tunisian.'
If we had the record of the passages of the last few months we could get at it exactly.

I can send it over to my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) if he wishes to examine it. He was asking the average time from Moville to Rimouski.
I have here the figures of the time of thirty trips from Rimouski to Moville. and I find. the average is seven days five hours.
Of all the mail boats ?
Yes. of all the mail boats.
What boats are in the mail service ?
The ' Bavarian,' * Tunisian,' Parisian,' Pretor-ian ' (occasionally), and the ' Ionian.'
What was the average speed of the ' Parisian ' and the ' Ionian ' ?
I do not think it is increasing by the Canadian route. I will have to apply to the Post Office for details, but I am certain there has been no material change.
You don't expect any material change from the Increased cost ?

I do not think so. I cannot venture to promise the House that there will be any alteration in that respect. We hope that with thoroughly comfortable and first-class boats there will be a considerable increase in the traffic, but I do not expect any increase in the mail matter and I Hunk the Post Office has cotne to that conclusion too. Heretofore the passage has ranged from seven to ten days, and it will be a very material improvement if we can establish on ocean ferry not exceeding six days.
Are we to understand that for all time to come a very large proportion of Canadian mail matter will go via New York ?

The average of the ' Parisian ' is nearly as fast as the ' Tunisian ' and the ' Bavarian.' The ' Ionian ' has made fair passages, but she is not quite as fast. I had a little memorandum made for my own information as to the relative cost of the various grades of steamers. The proportions are somewhat as follows :	15 knots would represent 34 ; 17
knot would represent 49 ;	20 knots would
represent 80, and 22 knots would represent 100. It is worth noting that the cost of 20 knots is very nearly double the cost of 17 knots. It is hoped the turbine system will enable us to get a greater speed at a less cost.
We are practically adding 50 per cent to get one knot, or one knot and a half increased speed.

About two knots. We propose that the 17 knot boats must do the service in six days and the others in six and a half days. The argument is that during the summer the two 17 knot steamers must make the passage in six days under penalties, and the ' Tunisian ' and 'Bavarian ' must not exceed seven days.
Does the minister expect that a larger proportion of the mail matter will go by the new steamers ?
I doubt. While New York is sending out one steamer per day, I think the bulk of our mail matter will go that way.
The figures given last session show that only one-seventh of our mail matter went by the Canadian route and the balance by New York.

It is not in my department precisely, but I am afraid that a very large proportion will always go by New York. They have a steamer per day and they are rather likely to increase than to diminish, and under these eir-cumstances we must make up our minds that a large proportion of our mail matter will go by that route.

A great object in having fast steamers between Canada and England is for the despatch of the mails. Whatever the reason for the change in public sentiment of recent years, the tendency of passengers going to Europe is to seek steamers which afford great comfort and accommodation, such as the ' Celtic ' and ' Cedric,' rather than great speed. If we only have a weekly steamer of very fast speed it does . not help us very much with reference to the mails. That is why it occurs to many people, that until we can have an extremely fast service between Canadian ports and European ports, we will not have very much use for a fast Atlantic service. If we had a three or four day service between Newfoundland and the -coast of Ireland there is no doubt that it would have a material effect on the carrying of the mails by such a route, and I should think passengers too. The 1 Tunisian ' and 1 Bavarian' now afford improved accommodation, and the securing of a large number of passengers through Canadian ports is a matter of some importance. I would like to ask the minister if he has made ample provision in the new contract in connection with these two turbine steamers, for really superior passenger accommodation ?

Yes. The Messrs. Allan have submitted the plans
ei63

to me and they have apparently made ample provision for the comfort and convenience of a very large number of passengers on these steamers.
What would be the time of these boats between Halifax and Moville ?
That is a winter trip, and twelve hours longer are allowed than to Rimouski.

The danger is that in coming to the banks of Newfoundland1' in thick foggy weather, when the banks are dotted with Ashing schooners, these steamers have to reduce their speed for the safety of themselves and the other craft in these waters. Sometimes the fog continues until you get into the St. Lawrence, and I am not so certain that the speed of steamers on that route can be very largely increased over the present rate.
Do I understand that the subsidies are given only to these four steamers-the two new ones and the ' Bavarian ' and the ' Tunisian ?' Or would any of the old steamers be included ?
(SMITH. All boats of the Allan Line't
All boats that are permitted to go ; but a special provision has been inserted that forty out of fifty-two trips must be performed by the new steamers or the ' Bavarian ' or the * Tunisian.'
Does the new contract cover all these vessels ?
It covers the two new steamers, with the ' Bavarian ' and ' Tunisian,' and as substitutes on occasion the ' Ionian ' and ' Parisian.'
What is the time fixed for the first sailing of the turbine steamers ?
One is to start during the month of August next, and the second one on or before the opening of navigation in the St. Lawrence river in the spring.
Is there any penalty attached for their failure to keep the dates ?

They are to receive a much larger subsidy, and the Messrs. Allan. I believe, have been pushing the construction of these vessels with all expedition. They have had some trouble from strikes, and I do not know that -we can depend on the vessel being delivered in the month of August. I am in correspondence with them on that subject now.
Are the vessels begun ?
Oh, yes. ' They are all but ready for delivery. My hon. friend is very incredulous.
We have been waiting a long time for that service.
Before the contract was signed w7e had notice that they were under way.
They are not like the dredges for Nova Scotia which have been under construction for the last three or four years, but are not finished yet.
That is the ' W. S. Fielding ' that my hon. friend is referring to ?
ROSS-(Victoria). Yes.

I suppose the hon. minister realizes that the people of Halifax, Sydney, St. John and other ports in the maritime provinces take a very great interest in this subject, and I would not like the impression to go abroad that the government have abandoned the idea of obtaining a really fast service.
Oh, no.

I rather judge, from what the hon. minister lias said, that he looks upon a modern, up-to-date, first-clpss service, as good as they have in New York, as something beyond the means of this government to provide. Last year, when this matter was up, the premier, I think, said that a thoroughly up-to-date service of twenty-two or twenty-three knots would cost us $1,500,000 a year, which he seemed to think was an outlay beyond the ability of this country. In the maritime provinces, at any rate, I am sure there would not be a ready acquiescence in that view. The people there believe that with the establishment of a service which would be equal in speed, efficiency and quality to that which runs to the port of New York, a large part of the passenger travel and a full supply of express freight would be carried through our ports in the maritime provinces. Therefore the people of Halifax and of those other ports regard it as a matter of great importance to them locally that such a service should be established. A great many take a larger view, however, and look upon it as a matter of national pride and interest. They believe it would have the effect of advertising Canada extensively, placing it on the line of through travel between Europe and Asia, diverting a. large part of the passenger travel of the world through Canadian territory, improving our position as a nation, placing us practically on the front street of the world's travel. That is a posi-I tion which we might hope to attain on ac-

count of our geographical position between the two great masses of the world's population, that is, the European and the eastern Asiatic. Such a service would attract a large portion of the travel which is in a hurry. While it must be admitted that a great many men are choosing the larger, steadier and more comfortable steamers when they wish to travel, there are always a large number of business men and others to whom every moment of time is of great value, and who will therefore always take the line that will give them the assurance of saving a few hours or days. The figures given by the minister show that the most he hopes to attain is an average speed of 14f knots.
That is putting it rather on the inside. In summer I hope to attain a great deal more.
Take the figures given by the hon. minister, that is what they average.

My hon. friend will note that the average is very materially reduced by any single vessel making a long passage. The ' Tunisian ' and ' Bavarian ' as a rule make the passage in six days and from ten to fifteen hours, which gives a decent average speed.

Suppose the minister gets an average of 15 knots. That is not a speed which will attract any travel. At that speed the vessels will not take our own mails if there is a change of sending them by a faster route. It may provide an express service, but it will not have the effect which we had hoped for, of giving us a service which will attract any large proportion of the world's passenger travel. It seems to me that the government of Canada should be perfectly willing to spend annually $1,500,000 to secure a really fast service. The large disbursements which would be made by these steamers in this country and by tourists making their way across Canada would largely reimburse the country for the expenditure necessary to provide the service. I hope the minister will give us the assurance that the government had not made up their mind that such a service is hopeless. At the time Mr. Dobell announced to this House that he had made up his mind that not more than 18 knots could be looked for, even such a statement was very disappointing to the House and the country ; but now' the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce assures us that the best this government can do after eight years is to provide a service of 15 knots, which is a liberal estimate of its speed. It really seems as if, instead of making progress, the government in those eight years have been going back. It is perfectly proper that we should recognize the difficulties in the way. They are enormous, and I suppose they are aggravated t'o a certain extent by the class of steamers to be employed. The introduction of the turbine steamers will to a certain extent involve delay. There are of course reasons why ship* owners should hesitate to put themselves to great expenditure, while this matter is still in the experimental stage, it is after all a disappointment to the people to find that instead of being able to realize the 20-knot service as promised in 1896, all that the minister can promise us, with an increased subsidy of $85,000, making $300,000 in all. is a 15-knot service. There is 50 per cent increase in the subsidy and no improvement in the service. It looks as if the matter were one the government are inclined to pooh-pooh, but I hope the minister* will make every effort to give the country the service we require.
It was partly in view of these considerations that I refused to extend the contract beyond two years, so that we might have time to do something in the direction the hon. gentleman proposes.

In what season of the year are the trips to be made by these faster
vessels ?
Chiefly during the summer months and the earlier part of the winter.

Then the slow boats will
do winter service ?
A portion of the time. It is not proposed that these vessels will all be laid off at the same time.
What will these slow boats receive per round trip ?
But those slow boats will not be on during the summer.
Does the hon. gentleman expect the passage will be made in six days from Rimouski to Moville ?
Yes, six days from the 1st of June to the 1st of November in each year covered by the agreement. ,
Does it require a 16-knot service to do that during the year ?
It would require a 17-knot service.

it is a very great improvement, because of these two new boats, one will have an average speed of 17 knots and the other will be somewhat faster. I understand that the second boat, which is being built, is likely to be a little speedier, but at any rate we are getting two boats with an average speed of 17 knots. They will be very superior boats. I have had the opportunity of looking at the specideations and diagrams and I consider they will be a great improvement to the service. While it is most desirable we should have the speediest service we can get, there is a good deal in what has been said by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), and that is that the travelling public to-day are looking more for comfort than for great speed. The favourite and most comfortable boats now running out of New York are the 'Cedric' and 'Arabic', and those large comfortable boats have not a speed of over 17 knots. Considering the condition of Canada and her population, if we are able to make from year to year, or every two years, a substantial advance towards securing these very fast steamers, we are accomplishing a great deal. It is a question whether a service of 17 or 18 knots would not be a service quite commensurate with the best interests of Canada. Of course if we could afford to have a daily ferry such as they have in New York, we would be in a position to attract a large proportion of the travel of the United states as well as of Canada, but we cannot hope to do that yet and it will be some time before we can.
How long ?

That will depend on the rapidity with which the country is opened up and advances. The trouble at Halifax was this, that the company could not secure freight for the larger steamers. The ' Tunisian ' and the ' Bavarian ' had to sail out of Halifax several times with very little cargo. Besides the loss of running the ship, there is the danger of navigating a light ship in winter, and the company were forced to put on smaller and inferior vessels. The ' Tunisian ' and ' Bavarian ' are good boats, well fitted up, and with twin screws, and the ' Parisian,' while older and smaller, has always been one of the favourite boats on the Atlantic route. I think we may congratulate ourselves that we have the improvements which are manifest in this contract. When we are able to ship our products of the west from our maritime ports, we will be in a position to secure the very fast and continuous service we are hoping for, and we are confident that will be realized in the near future.

The hon gentleman's logic is defective. The minister says that these fast boats are not good freight carriers, but the hon. gentleman says that when we are able to secure the freight from the ' Mr. WADE.
west we will have the fast boats. Which is right ?
I think I can make the hon. gentleman understand.
He was trying to put in a bar for the Grand Trunk Pacific.

Not necessarily. I will make my hon. friend understand by telling him that all big steamship companies run their very fast boats at a loss and make up the loss on their other business with their other boats. Not one of these ocean greyhounds, which run out of New York, is run at a profit, but the profit on the company's other business compensates for the loss on the swift boats.
Speaking from recollection, I think the average passage is two or three days less.
I understood the right hon. gentleman to say that the average passage to-day was eight or ten days.
No, I said that the average rate in summer was seven days.

I understood the minister to say that these new steamers would be so much in advance of the ordinary rate to-day that the difference would be practically the difference between ten days and seven days.
I was referring to the old times.
But he was speaking of the work done by the steamers in use today, the ' Bavarian ' and ' Tunisian.'
They have not taken ten days or anything like it.

He told us that the average speed was 144 knots an hour. That was the very best he could say, and. after carefully revising his calculation, he said it would be 141 knots, or, perhaps it would be
safe to say 14 knots. That does not seem to me to be much in advance of what it was.
The hon. gentleman will find that the average rate is considerably in advance of what it was seven years ago.
Will the right hon. gentleman give us some data showing on what he bases that statement ?
A few years ago the passages were made in eleven, twelve or thirteen days-eleven was rather exceptional.
What ships made that rate ?

The ships of the various lines. We changed the service once or twice. Some of the Allan liners, some of the Dominion and some of the Beaver liners were employed. But they certainly were very inferior in point of speed to the average of the present day.
Of course, the right hon. gentleman has the data on which that statement is made or he would not make it ? Will he be kind enough to bring the data before the committee .?
Yes.
Let us have it at three o'clock.

Another element in the situation that we ought not to overlook is this : Under the present system people coming to Canada from across the Atlantic generally land in New York-in a foreign country. They pass through the great state of New York, and sometimes a great many other states, before they reach Canada. Many of these are intending investors, and, seeing the advantages of the United States and the attractions for investment there, they are apt to be induced to invest their money in the United States instead of in Canada. Why should we land our passengers in a foreign country ? If they landed in Canada and went four thousand miles across our country before reaching the Pacific, they could not but be impressed with the advantages offered by Canada for investment of capital. It seems to me that it w'ould be of incalculable advantage to us to have passengers coming to Canada land in Canada direct.
How can you compel people to land in Canada ?

You cannot compel them, but if you will bring them quicker into Canada directly than via New York they will come in by the faster line. If I start from Toronto to come to Ottawa to do business. and there are three trains a day and one goes a little faster than the other, I

will of course take the fastest one. So it is with a business man. We are living in a fast age, in an age of speed, and we will take the fastest trains and the fastest line of steamers.
But people who cross the Atlantic ocean generally do it for pleasure, and they prefer to go through a foreign port.

I said there was a percentage who travelled for pleasure, and in that case I presume they would look rather for comfort than speed. But the great enterprising business class of men, which is of value to us because they make their investments here, are the people that we should invite to land upon our shores instead of landing in New York before they reach Canada. These are considerations of immense value to the Canadian people, and we are not equal to the occasion if we allow this state of things to go on from year to year that has been going the last seven years, without any substantial improvement except what we are offered to-day in the shape of these two new steamers that are to be built, and even these I understand are only an experiment.
I do not wish the hon. gentleman to misquote me before the committee. I did not say that the ' Bavarian ' and the ' Tunisian ' were fast enough, I said they were satisfactory to us.
X understood the hon. member to say that the service had proved satisfactory to the public.

I said nothing of the kind, I said these two boats, the ' Tunisian ' and the ' Bavarian,' were satisfactory to the people, and the ' Parisian ' was an old favourite, these two boats as compared with the others would be a distinct improvement in the service and one that would be pleasing to the people. The hon. gentleman also said we had slow boats enough for carrying grain and freight. That is all very well, we have slow boats enough for carrying freight, but where is the freight to put in them ? The freight was not there last winter, and as a consequence they could not run these large boats, the ' Bavarian ' and the ' Tunisian,' and they had to put on the ' Laurentian,' the ' Pretorian ' and boats of that kind. Now if we can get freight to these ocean ports which will fill the slower boats, it will build up the business of the country and the company can afford to run swifter boats. Now with regard to the pretention of the hon. gentleman that the people -want to travel by swift boats, he is entirely mistaken,

I did not make any such statement. I said no doubt those who travel for pleasure would look for comfort rather than speed, but I said that the great enterprising business class of men desired to go by the fastest boats.

I think I know something about the desires of people who travel across the Atlantic on pleasure bent. The hon. gentleman is quite wrong. There is a certain class of business men who need to travel in great haste and will take the fastest line, but the great mass of the travelling public I am speaking about are looking principally for comfortable boats, which are not what we style ocean greyhounds. Now if we can 'secure two of these boats for this service running to Canada, it is going to be a great benefit, and a great advantage in other directions, it is going to improve the service. This contract expires at the end of two years, after which we may be able to make still more progress than we are making now. As I said before, if we are able to carry our products to the ocean ports for shipment there so that we can give these boats business and trade, there is no doubt but that we will get in due time the fast service that we are all so anxious to secure.

The hon. member evidently misunderstood me, at least he misrepresents me. I had not a word of complaint with regard to the proposed new steamers, because I think they are certainly a great improvement on the old ones, they are faster. But what I complain of is that we have made so little headway during the last seven years, and that the best that is offered us to-day are two more boats that will make but little better speed than the old ones.

As far as the item under consideration is concerned it doesn't make much difference as to whether people prefer to travel by a slow boat or a fast boat. We are asked to add fifty per cent to the sum that has been voted for mail subsidies, and we are only getting an accelerated speed of a knot and a half in the hour. The question is what will be the result so far as the mail service is concerned from this increased expenditure of $85,000 ? It will result in increasing the average speed by a knot or a knot and a half an hour, and that is all. What is the advantage to be gained by the people from this $85,000 of additional expenditure ? This subsidy, as I understand, is given for the carriage of the mails ; but if the mails continue to pass through the New York post office for the purpose of being transmitted to the old country by a faster line than we can offer, what advantage are we going to get ? That is what we want to get at. The question is not whether the people prefer to travel by a slow boat or a fast one ; we want to know what advantage we are going to derive from this fifty per cent additional expenditure so far as the carriage of the mails in concerned ? If the mails are to be sent via New York what advantage are we to obtain from this increased subsidy ? Before the item passes, I would

like the hon. gentleman to bring us the particulars of the acceleration of speed which has been accomplished during the past eight years. We have, I think, a record of the average speed for the year before last; we want to see wherein the average time of crossing has been reduced during the past eight years. The hon. gentleman must have these particulars in his office, and when the committee resumes at three o'clock I hope he will be able to give them to us.

I will
see what we have.
At one o'clock, committee took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.

speechtext: The subject before the committee is the further consideration of resolution 153, ocean and mail service between Great Britain and Canada.

Before we proceed with the discussion of this item, might I ask the minister whether it is true that an official of the department .has been sent up to Sarnia, to the Standard Oil Refinery, to look after the interests of the producers ?

An
official was sent up to report on the best method of distributing the bounty, if that is what my hon. friend refers to.
Then I understand that instead of going to the producing district, the agent was sent to the Standard refinery to find out the best way of distributing the bounty.
I understand he went ail over.
What might I under stand from ' all over ' ?
He went to both parties, the refiners and the producers, and examined the mode of production in the district generally.
Did he go to Pet-rolea ?
Yes.
The information I have is very different.
I can only give the information that I have received from the department that he was there.

Has the minister been able to procure a statement as to the average time and average speed of the vessels during the last six or eight years ? The right hon. gentleman said that the time had been cut down by two or three days.
I was referring more particularly lo xhe time made in 1895 and 1897.
Will we be able to get a return for the average time in 1895 and 1897 and the names of the ships ?
I have not the names of the ships. But from Mo-ville to Halifax in 1895 they took ten days and ten hours on the average, in 1897 ten days and 22 hours.
That was an improvement in favour of 1895 as against 1897. Has the hon. gentleman the times for the years since 1897 ?
No. I have not the time for the whole period.
In view of that statement that the time has been reduced by two or three days from what it was in 1896 it would be well to have it.
I shall get that but it may take some little time to procure it.

Has the minister a reasonable assurance that as the result of this new contract with the Allans and the increase of the subsidies by $85,000 a year, the Canadian mails will go by these ships from Canadian ports ?
A certain proportion but not more.

If the right hon gentleman has not a reasonable assurance that as a result of this increased subsidy of $85,000 a year the Canadian mails will go by Canadian ships what p rticular advantage is there ?

course it is open to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) to move to return to the old condition if he likes. The advantage is that we get a much better service than ever before for passengers and freight and incidentally for the mails. The hon. gentleman knows very well that we do not profess or pretend that this will bring us any lhrge additional proportion of the mails ; I do not think that it is to be looked for. So long as there is a daily service from New York, as I have explained again and again, the vast proportion of the mails will go by New York and not by Canadian lines.
For these vessels running 17 knots.
The two turbines ?[DOT]
Yes.'

The right hon. minister says that fresh contracts have been made within the last year. Has he made any provision to protect the shippers in regard to freight rates ? Are the freight rates to be in the future as in the past season very much higher out of Montreal than on boats from New York, even although we subsidize these boats to the exteut of $10,000 for each trip of the new boats ?

There is a provision under which control can be exercised over them, but I cannot pretend to isay that we will be able to obtain as low raltes from Montreal as from New York. At the present time, as the hon. gentleman probably knows, the rates from Montreal are very low indeed, lower than from New York.

There is very little freight going now and when there is little freight offered the boats always lower the rates. It is when a large cargo is going over that it is of the utmost importance to the producers that the rates ^should be as low as possible, but that is the time the steamboats raised the rates, when they could really afford to carry cheaper. The hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) complains that these boats get light cargoes from Halifax and St. John. That was not the case from Montreal last year ; they went out fully loaded, but the rates were 20 per cent higher than out of Boston and New York, and I would submit that in making these contracts where large subsidies are given, the government might protect the producers in that by stipulating as has been done in some cases that they should not charge a higher rate than is charged by vessels of similar speed from Boston, New York or Portland, and I submit that unless that has been done in this case, a very great injustice has been done to the producer. The minister stated also that cold storage was to be provided on these two new boats.
Yes.
I believe there is already cold storage on the other boats. Is there any provision in the contracts with regard to the temperature in these cold storage chambers ?

The Minister of Agriculture defines proper cold storage.
Mr: E. D. SMITH. The Minister of Agriculture states that it is impossible for him Mr. CLARKE.
to control the temperature of these cold storage chambers after the original contract expired. There was an opportunity when these contracts were made to obtain absolute control by the Minister of Agriculture of t'he temperature of these chambers.
The stipulation is for cold storage, but there is no particular provision as to temperature.

That is the essential feature of cold storage. Cold storage is of very little use, indeed, unless the temperature is absolutely as required for the various commodities that are shipped. In fact it is not cold storage at all in the proper sense unless it is almost perfect and kept at the mark required by the various commodities that go forward. The producers and shippers complain that although large sums have been spent by the government in assisting steamships to provide cold storage still there is no control whatever over the chambers. On some vessels and on some voyages the temperature is absolutely correct. The stuff is carried over under proper conditions but on others again it is a long way from being perfect, and the Minister of Agriculture complains that he has no control and no power. It seems to me that if he has no power, if these contracts have expired, there was an opportunity in the making of these contracts to secure proper control.
So far as the Allan Line was concerned, no complaints were made to us as to cold storage. I am not prepared to speak as to the other vessels that had cold storage accommodation.

I may say that they are a long way from being perfect. Some are very good, but many are far, far from perfect or what they ought to be, and the only way we can be assured that the temperature will be properly kept is for the government to have an absolute control over the cold storage. If the government have control over one line and can assure the shippers that they will get proper accommodation on one line, then of course the other lines which do not get subsidies will have to do the same thing or they would not get the trade. When the government is giving this subsidy to the one line and making this contract they have an opportunity to absolutely control the situation.
In case the cold storage is imperfect I have power to reduce the subsidy under the terms of the contract.

Perhaps a more important matter than the cold storage is the ventilation of these ships. Almost all our cheese, which is one of our chief articles

of export, and our apples go over, not in cold storage and not in what we call cool air storage, but in the ordinary holds of the vessels, which ought to he ventilated. It is a very small matter to secure that ventilation and it appears to me that the government have no power over the steamships in this matter. All that has been done apparently is that the Minister of Agriculture has sent a letter asking the steamship companies to properly ventilate the holds. Some have done this and others have not. There was an opportunity when these contracts were being made to provide for ventilation of the holds. I would like to ask the minister if that has been done.

With regard to this particular line of steamships the apple shippers of Nova Scotia are not so much concerned ; they do not carry very many of the apples from Nova Scotia, inasmuch as their destination is Liverpool, while our market is London. . With regard to New Brunswick, I have heard of no complaint except in one case, that of a steamship which was in distress and put in at the Azores, with the result that her cargo was landed in bad condition. The Canadian , Pacific Railway boats and other lines that carry fruit have landed their cargoes in good condition, and no complaint has been made about them. I would like to see the government retain a control over the rates charged by the steamship lines. I do not know anything about the rates on grain, but I think the government should have some control over the freight rates on fruit.
1 take exception to the statement made by the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Clarke), that this vote is for a mail subsidy alone. It is a subsidy for a mail and a steamship service, and I think the freight service which we are able to obtain is very important, and should be well looked after. So far as my province is concerned, I must say that very good work has been done as regards the shipment of fruit. The stringency cf the provisions of the contract which the government has exacted from the steamship people lias compelled them to carry the fruit over in a very much better condition than formerly. lLast year it gave absolute satisfaction, except in the case of one steamer, to which I have directed the ministers attention.
How does the hon gentleman know that fruit and apples and cheese are carried over in such perfect con-ditto n ?
I did not speak of cheese ; I referred to the apples shipped from the province of Nova Scotia and from New Brunswick.
How does the hon. gentleman know ?

I know it in the same way you would know anything ; from informa-1974
tion I have gathered. I have been at pains to inquire. I have been on the docks in London and have seen the fruit delivered Irom the steamers. I have been at the market, and have seen the fruit there. I have conversed with the leading shippers throughout the Annapolis valley, and from their testimony I am justified in forming my opinion.
Is this subsidy given for the shipping of apples, or is it a mail subsidy ? What we want to know is what advantage the country will get from this additional mail subsidy of $85,000.

The steamship lines that carry the bulk of the fruit from Nova Scotia are the Furness-Withy and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and a sun-sidy has been granted to them. I do not say that they do not get any cargoes in St. John or Halifax. I said they did not get sufficient cargo, and that is a fact. I went over in the ' Pretorian ' myself when she had only one-third of a cargo, and I speak feelingly on the matter, because the steamer rolled a good deal in consequence.

The hon. gentleman 'Mr Wade) seems to think that because he saw some apples landed in good condition on the other side, our shipments of apples have been carried over in perfect condition. The fact is that, although a good many mules may have been carried over in good condition, there also have been a good many carried over in bad condition.
From Nova Scotia ?
Yes.
What ship delivered her cargo in bad shape, and whose fruit did she carry ?

I could give the hon. gentleman the information with a little trouble. Some of these same steamers went from Montreal and the ventilation was not much changed in the meantime. It is a very easy matter to prove this by putting one thermograph where the fruit is carried and another thermograph on deck, so that the temperatures might be compared. The Minister of Agriculture told us that he had no power to control the ventilation on these vessels, but the time to get that power is when you are making these contracts. The contract has now been made for another two years, and there is no provision made that the Minister of Agriculture or his officers shall have power to board these vessels and see that the regulations are enforced. Again the government have let the opportunity -slip by them.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce has announced that he is satisfied with an Atlantic service of about fourteen and a half knots, and he has

also announced that we will have to content ourselves with the fact that possibly for all time to come the bulk of our mails will be carried by way of New York. I do not accept either of these propositions as being correct; and I do not think the people of Canada will calmly agree that we are not to have a fast Atlantic service, or that the bulk of the Canadian mail matter must be carried by New York. In 189G both political parties had committed themselves to a fast Atlantic service, and the Conservative government before leaving office had made a contract for such a service by steamers of 20 knots or 21 knots an hour. That is confirmed by a statement made last session by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and which is reported in ' Hansard.' page 14161. When the Liberal government came to power, for reasons which have never been satisfactorily explained to the country, they saw fit to put an end to the proposed arrangement with the Allans, and they told us that they would secure faster vessels with better accommodation for passengers and freight. Accordingly, in 1S97, the minister (Sir Richard Cartwright) brought down a resolution with reference to the Petersen contract.
At that time the present government thought that any service of less than twenty or twentyone knots was too slow, and that it was an absolute necessity in the interest of the country that we should have a fast service. What did the hon. gentlemen then promise to the country ? They promised to furnish steamships of 10,000 gross registered tons instead of 8,500 tons, and to maintain on the line from port to port across the Atlantic an average speed of 500 knots per day, or twenty-one knots per hour. They promised, in connection with such service and forming part thereof, to provide and maintain fast tenders of the torpedo-boat type, of a speed of not less than twenty-two knots per hour, to meet the steamers on their apjiroach to Canada, to act as pilot boats, so as to ensure in the navigation of such ships both safety and speed, and that the said steamships should be constructed, fitted and maintained in all respects equal to the best Atlantic steamers now afloat. That contract was said to have been consummated, and it was represented on that occasion, not only by the right hon. gentleman who introduced it, but by those who followed him. that it was absolutely necessary in the interest of the country. To-day we. not only have the right hon. gentleman intimating that we shall have to put up with having the mails of this countrv carried by American vessels, but that 14j'knots an hour is a respectable service for Canada [DOT] and we have other hon. gentlemen-for instance, the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) saying that it is a mistake for any government to think that a fast Atlantic service is desirable-that what the people

want is slow and gentle travelling-not to go very rapidly, but to go with exceptional comfort. What the Petersen contract was said to secure was both exceptional comfort, high-class travelling, and a speed of twenty-one knots an hour. That we had secured that was announced by the right hon. gentleman who leads the House, in a speech which he made on the 6th of October, 1897, in the city of Toronto. With a considerable flourishing of trumpets he said that we were going to have an immediate end put to the Americans carrying the'mails of Canada, and Canada was going to secure her own carrying trade and also the carrying trade of a great portion of the western states as well. This is what the right hon.-gentleman said on that occasion :
Sir Frank Smith's government had undertaken to give to that service a bonus, a subsidy, of $750,000 a year. We thought it was too much. We thought we could do it for less, and we succeeded in making a contract with a firm for a subsidy of $500,000, saving to the country therefore the sum of $250,000. We contracted with the firm of Petersen, Tate &- Co., a Newcastle firm, a firm rcm-' posed as we ascertained, of men of the highest. honour, of the highest integrity, and the highest competency in their profession.
This is almost like the Transcontinental Railway question. When the right hon. gentleman speaks of any man with whom he makes contracts, he always refers to him as a man of the highest integrity, the highest honour, and the highest qualities of every kind. But in the case of the Transcontinental Railway it may turn out as did that of the fast Atlantic service, that he had not investigated as fully as he thought. The right hon. gentleman went on to say :
Mr. Petersen and Mr. Tate have had a good many obstacles to overcome, as is always the case with men who launch a new idea into the world. Their idea was a new one, and therefore it met with objections and with discouragement from more than one class of people ; and not later than a few few weeks ago, or a few days ago only it was stated that the scheme of Mr. Petersen had fallen down, that it must he considered as absolutely a thing of the past. Mr. Petersen and Mr. Tate were at work. They work as men always work when they want to succeed. They said nothing ; they answered no accusations ; but to-day I have a telegram from my friend and colleague, Mr. Fielding, the Minister of Finance, to this effect :
' Petersen has made to-day the deposit required by the contract.' (Loud cheering and great enthusiasm.)

Clause 14 of the contract reads :
The steamers employed in carrying out the provisions of this contract, shall not on any voyages either outwards or inwards, call at any foreign port not specified in this contract.

That would be quite sufficient to prevent them going to Portland. As a matter of fact it would be practically impossible for them to do so and carry out the terms of the contract.

That is not the case. I believe the Allans do run ships to Portland, but not these ships.

The government do not undertake to supply them with cargoes ; they must do that for themselves.
They are not bound to go to St. John if they cannot get sufficient cargo there ?
They may be excused. Of course they will desire to obtain cargo at St. John if they possibly can.
They might desire much more to obtain it somewhere else.
Then they could only obtain it in Halifax.
Yes ; the contract provides that they must go either to Halifax or St. John, and the government can only excuse them from going to one place or the other.
As I understand the contract these steamers must call at Halifax in winter under any circumstance, and at the discretion of the minister they may be required to go to St. John.
I would put it the other way ; they must go to St. John and Halifax, but they may be excused under certain conditions from going to St. John.
Under what circumstances would the minister excuse the steamers from calling at St. John ?

I would excuse them only when it became perfectly evident that they could not obtain cargo at St. John. The Canadian Pacific Railway have a line of their own at St. John to which most probably they will give the preference. It has happened, perhaps owing to snowdrifts or other causes, that there has been absolutely no cargo at St. John in one or two cases ; I hope that will not often happen, but it would be only in an extreme case that this clause of the contract would be invoked.

The minister told us that it would be practically impossible for these vessels to carry out their contract and go to Portland. I do not think that statement can be sustained. It is more than likely that the ' Bavarian ' or the ' Tunisian ' would alternate with one of the turbine boats, which would give each of these vessels two weeks to cross the Atlantic, and as they are bound to make the voyage from Moville to St. John or Halifax in seven and a half days they would have no difficulty in proceeding from one of these Canadian ports to Portland.

They would have to stay a certain time at St. John or Halifax, and I do not think they could carry out their contract if they called at Portland. Even if the hon. gentleman were correct in his contention. I hold that the contract prevents them from going to Portland at all.
Then the minister is satisfied that the contract binds them not to go to Portland.
I do not think there is the slightest intention on their part to go to Portland and I certainly would call them to task if they did.

When the hon. gentleman's estimates were under consideration last year, we made some statements as to discrimination in rates, and, if my memory serves me, the hon. gentleman sent some of his officers to Boston and other points in the eastern states to ascertain if it was a fact that discrimination was used against Canadian shippers and in favour of foreign shippers. Has the hon. gentleman the report of his officers who made that inquiry, and if so, what did they find ?
I know that the inquiry was made.

I think the hon. gentleman is in error on that point.

There was another reason why it seemed probable. for Canadians for a certain length of time, but that if the whole cargo was not obtained within that time, the vessel was to receive freight from wherever it could get it. The hon. gentleman's answer was : What can we do ? I am afraid it is almost impossible to avoid that.

The statement I made in the House last year was based on informal tion which was obtained from shippers and published from time to time in the newspapers. In one of the Toronto papers, I think the ' News,' there appeared a special despatch of the 23rd of February last, from its correspondent in Montreal, in which it was stated :

Maelunes, freight traffic manager of the Canadian Pacific Railway, was asked yesterday whether it were true that the Canadian Pacific Railway were giving shippers in United States manufacturing centres a better rate to Vancouver than was given to shippers in Montreal and Toronto. He replied that the rate on such American shipments would be a slight advance on the rate from the same American port to Seattle, the exact advance depending on the classification. Before one o'clock I asked the hon. minister in regard to the prospect of more Canadian mail matter being carried through Canadian ports. I understood him to say that there was no prospect of an improvement in that direction. Since the recess he has qualified that to a certain extent, and I would now ask him what is the prospect of an increased proportion of our mail service going by Canadian routes instead of such a large proportion going by United States routes ?

The department despatches mails to England by the quickest route. There are not vessels leaving Canada every day, and if the despatching of letters via American ports will result in their reaching their destination sooner than if detained for Canadian vessels, they will be sent through the American ports. I suppose the same rule is adopted by foreign post offices in'despatching mails to Canada. The greater the improvement in our own service, .the more mail matter will be sent by our own route. I understand that the Allans are building a turbine steamer which will have a speed of 17 knots per hour. That will be a considerable advance in speed over any of our present steamers and will cause a good deal of the mails, destined for eastern Canada at least, to come by our route instead of via New York. As to the mails for points west of Montreal, it would be rather difficult by any improvement in our own steamship service to get them into Ontario more quickly by Canada than by New York. There will always be a good deal of mail matter go by New York simply because you do not have steamers leaving on the Canadian route every day.
What will be the difference in time in the case of a letter leaving Montreal by the Canadian route and one leaving New York ?
It would depend upon what steamships were sailing.
Assuming the average mail service from New York and Canada.

Take the Allan Line, which sails from Montreal on Friday.	The malls are put on
board at Rimouski, which is 130 miles east of Quebec and 250 east of Montreal. That steamer which takes those mails Saturday morning will reach perhaps Movilie in about a week from that day or on Sunday morning, and the mails will not be in London before Monday morning. If they were sent by New York and happened to catch the ' Campania ' or ' Lueania,' of the Cunard Line, they might reach London Saturday morning. Sometimes those two steamers reach Queenstown on Friday night. If they do, it is sometimes the practice of the English post office, which controls the handling of the mails, to have special trains waiting at Queenstown. The mails are put on shore there and sent from Ireland across by the fast packet, and they will reach London on Saturday morning. That, however, is a comparatively rare occurrence. The mails usually remain on board and only reach London on Saturday afternoon at the earliest. If on the other hand those letters were sent from New York by the steamers ' Umbria ' and ' Etruria,' they would not reach London any quicker than by the Canadian route.
Are we to understand that speaking generally there is an advantage of about forty-eight hours in favour of New York ?

It is not possible to speak about averages when you have vessels of entirely different speed and there are other disturbing circumstances. On the whole the mails that leave Canada by the Allan Line and those that go via New York reach London pretty much the same time. There are chances of the mails from New York reaching London on Saturday, but they are not always realized, and we prefer to give the public the benefit of those chances.

Are we to understand that it is only by chance that the mails leaving New York reach London quicker than by a Canadian port ? If that be true, it is difficult to understand why such a large portion is sent by New York.

It takes longer for a letter to go from Toronto to Rimouski than from Toronto to New York. You can post a letter in Toronto on Friday and it may catch the outgoing steamers on Saturday morning at New York, but if you wanted that letter to catch the steamer at Rimouski, it would have to be posted at Toronto much earlier.

It is amusing to hear the hon. gentleman talking about the failure of Petersen ; it would be more correct to regard it as the failure of the government. We were then told that the $750.000 annual subsidy which had been proposed by the late Conservative administration, was absolutely absurd and unnecessary, that the proposal could not be carried out, and that this government could accomplish it at once at a saving to the country each year, for twenty years, of $250,000, or $5,000,000 altogether. Of which $250,000 was furnished by the government of Great

Britain. The original proposal was $750,000 of an annual subsidy for 20 years by this government, which was to be supplemented by one-half that amount for the same period of time as an annual grant by the imperial government, making altogether $1,125,000 per annum of a subsidy. Well, this government said that was too much, they would not entertain that proposal, they would not go on with it, although the contract was with the very company was then ready, subject to a short delay to enable them to make their arrangements, to carry out that proposal. The proposal was deemed an extravagant one, $500,000 a year was considered ample, and we were treated to the bottle-necked vessels proposal, which was announced as an accomplished fact by the Prime Minister in Toronto after he had received a conveniently timed telegram from the Minister of Finance. Now some six years after, after the fast Atlantic service has been dropped by the government-because that was the effect of the statement of the Postmaster General last year-we are coming back to a proposal for a subsidy of $330,000 a year for a service of 17 knots for two steamers in the summer, and something less in the winter, and a service of 14 knots for the other steamers. I do not know whether my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce feels inclined to congratulate himself upon this magnificent result of eight years effort by a businesslike government. I am inclined to think that if he were disposed to congratulate himself upon this result, he would not find very much' company among the people of Canada. I think it is a very pitiable result of all the efforts of this government for eight years, that we are now paying two-thirds of the amount which they said was amply sufficient for a fast service, and they are paying it for what would be regarded in New York as no better than a third-class service so far as speed is concerned. There may be some consideration present to our minds which should make us realize the importance of what one might call a fast freight service as well as a fast passenger service. But it has been the policy of the government as I understand, until within the last two years at least, to establish a fast Atlantic service, regarding it of so much importance that the Prime Minister himself was selected to hearld the consummation of that project to the city of Toronto and the country. Now, either they have changed their minds or they have made a bad mess of it. I can appeal with confidence to the Minister of Trade and Commerce to join with me in that regret, because I know his own mind with regard to it. orders represented that should the scheme be put through this coming session, it will be very popular with all classes of railway employees ; and your help will be much appreciated by all concerned.
