I trust that the minister will have a comprehensive scheme brought forward that will do justice to the men employed on the government railways. As to the conduct of the Prince Edward Island Railway, the vote for which is now before us, we are not at all satisfied with the management in many respects. I had occasion to wait upon the minister at one time myself and bring to his attention a case of gross inattention to the interests of farmers and working men of an important part of Prince Edward Island as well as of failure to properly manage the affairs of the road. I refer to the distribution of cars for the haulage of mussel mud and wood, two large industries carried on in the western part of Prince Edward Island. I gave the minister at that time some statistics in regard to the carriage of these products. The mussel mud is used as a manure by the farmers, and is a very necessary element to keep their land in condition. It is very extensively used along the whole length of the line. There are quite a number of truckmen and labourers engaged in digging this mud and hauling it to the railway. During the greater part of last winter, when they should have had twenty-seven cars per day, they had twenty-seven cars per week to carry this material. And this occurred in spite of the protests made. I myself wrote on several occasions to the superintendent, but got no relief for the men. It was not until I came up to interview the minister and when the winter was practically over and the wages of these men had been lost for the season that some relief was promised. Not only was this the case in mussel mud, but it was the case in the haulage of cord wood. In many cases people on the western end of the line had to put their cord wood in box cars to get it to the selling point. Now, this is, possibly, a matter of small import to the Minister of Railways and Canals and to this government, but it affects very materially the class of labourers and others who are dependent on this industry for their livelihood. I understand that there were ample cars on the road if proper foresight had been used in sending them where they were needed.
I understand the cars were on the Murray Harbour branch, and early in the season the superintendent promised to have these cars brought over and put into this service, but they were never brought over. The excuse given at the end of the winter was that there was a snow blockade, but even if there liad been, it was not heavy enough to prevent a business management from operating the cars and putting them

at the disposal of those men. This is a state of affairs that I trust the present Minister of Railways will look into more carefully than he had occasion to at the time. The people are not at all satisfied with the explanation given by the superintendent of the Prince Edward Island Railway, nor do I myself believe that it was a legitimate excuse for the shortage of cars in that locality during the whole winter. There is another matter I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Railways, and that is the fact that the service from Boston and western Canada down to Prince Edward Island via Point du Chene-the largest part of the tourist traffic and the largest part of the summer travel goes to Prince Edward Island by this route-has been for years past disgraceful. It is not certainly up to the equipment on any other branch of the Intercolonial, and is not fit for the growing travel to Prince Edward Island at the present time. The cars which run from Point dn Chene down, are not certainly of a class to induce the better class of tourists to patronize that line. They are usually the oldest cars on the line. There are no parlour cars that western travellers can take. I have a communication from the Charlottetown Development and Tourist Association, dated July 5th, asking that this matter be brought to the attention of the minister, and with the permission of the House I will read the letter and the resolution :
Sir,-At a meeting of the executive of this association held last evening, the inclosed resolution was passed, and copies thereof ordered to be forwarded to the Minister of Railways, to the members of parliament for this province, and to D. Pottinger, Esq., general manager Canadian government railways. I have been instructed to respectfully state that the resolution was moved because of several complaints reaching members of our executive with refereence to (1) the lack of accommodation obtainable in brst-elass coaches between St. John and Point du Chene.
To whom is that addressed ?
This letter is addressed to me.
The resolution ?
The resolution was sent to the Minister of Railways.
Who sent it. and when ?

The letter is dated July 5fh. and the resolution was passed and copies were forwarded, as I understand to the Minister of Railways, to the general manager of the Canadian government railways and to members of parliament.
(2) the necessity of providing a parlour car upon the road between these points.
This is a very necessary step, because people travel in parlour cars from the United
States and from the western provinces, they have parlour cars nearly all the way down, except over that strip of line. As the minister knows, the strength of a chain is its weakest link, and there is a weak link in this road running down from St. Jehn and Painsec to Point du Chene.
(3) because of the difficulty some travellers have experienced in obtaining information regarding the departure of trains from St. John to Point du Chene. This resolution is therefore respectfully submitted in the hope that you will do what you can to have the matter arranged in a manner more beneficial to the interests of this province.
I am, sir, your obedient servant,
A. C. IRWIN, Secretary.
Now it is a fact that this state of things has been protested against for years but apparently the difficulty has not been removed. This not only occurs in winter but in the summer time.
The resolution reads as follows :
Resolved, that in the opinion of the Charlottetown Development and Tourist Association, it is desirable to have a parlour car run through from Boston to Point du Chdne each day during the continuance of the through train, the present service being wholly inadequate and detrimental to summer travel to Prince Edward Island.
I bring this forward with due respect to the minister and the general manager, in the hope that they will look into fihese matters. I think the minister will realize that the travel coming there now, and which is increasing. requires more attention than has been afforded it over that portion of the line. I had occasion last year to speak of the extension of the railway along the water front in Charlottetown. I understand that nothing definite has been arrived at-by the government in this respect. The last two years I have been bringing this to the attention of the government, and the people of Charlottetown, the board of trade, and the city council are a unit on the necessity for this work. The merchants lliroughout the whole island who have to use the Charlottetown wharfs for the transhipment of their goods to different points on the island, are put to an expense that is not fair to them, they are inconvenienced in the transhipment of their goods along the Prince Edward Island Railway, and they have been working for this extension for a number of years. I submit that Phis Is a matter that cannot wait, we cannot wait five or six years more for these improvements that the people demand at once. Also in respect to the railway station the minister said the hole was being filled up for a railway station. I understood he stated in the House the other day they had not decided on a location for the railway station ; then why are they filling in this hole before the location is decided upon. A great majority of the better class of the people of Charlottetown, the board of

trade and the town council, have petitioned and sent resolutions and deputations to the minister, asking that the station be located at the intersection of Great George and Water streets, where the land is much higher and more available in the interests of Charlottetown than where the station is at present located. I understand that various offers have been made to the government of land, and that the prices are not unreasonable. But there are some political interests at work to have the railway down near the old station where it is at the present time, and the government are trying to keep the political strings dangling as long as possible before they decide where the depot shall be. Now I think there is only one possible place t'liat will suit the people of Charlottetown and that will at the same time be advantageous to the interests of the Prince Edward Island Railway.
I think the minister should not hesitate to have the station built at this point. There has been some talk of engineering difficulties but I have found the consensus of opinion among engineers of repute who understand the situation thoroughly to be that there are no engineering difficulties in the way. Besides that the railway would have to be brought to this point in being extended along the water front and part of the increased cost of putting the station at George and Water streets would necessarily go to the extension of the line along the water front. Then too the Marine Department has purchased a wharf there for the improvement of the government property and of the facilities at this wharf it would be advisable to extend the line that far. From the estimates I find that the minister has added an amount for Kinkora station. I pressed this on the minister for a number of years and I was very glad to have him look into the matter with me last year in a very reasonable way and insert the item and I am glad to see that he has included an item for establishing a station at this point. I pressed on the minister at that time the necessity for having a booking station there.
I trust that the additional $150 which I see in the estimates this year is for the establishment of a booking station at that point. Is that correct ?

There is $150 in the supplementaries for a station at Kinkora. The lowest tenders exceeded the estimate of the department and the appropriation so that we had to increase the amount. The question of a booking station at that point has been under the consideration of the department, but the business at that station as shown by the returns would hardly justify making it a booking station. When the trade and prospects of the place would justify it the department would hope to establish a booking station there.

I went fully into this question with the minister several months ago and I stated to him exactly the situation there. I think he was visibly impressed with the necessity of having a booking station at that point. The inconvenience to shippers at this point is so great that they are practically unable to carry on their commercial intercourse with the rest of the island unless they secure a booking station.

When my hon. friend brought that matter to my attention and it was also pressed on me by other hon. members from the island I referred the matter to the officials of the government railways and their report was to the effect which I have just stated. I do not know anything about the matter personally ; I know that my hon. friend said that in his judgment there should be a booking station, but there are always these differences of opinion between outsiders and the officials. I must be guided in these matters by the judgment of the officials who are the ones who should know something about them.

I must contend that it is not fair for the management to take into consideration only the monetary returns from a station in a case of this kind. They should take into account tire inconvenience that is caused to the people by the lack of accommodation. I must insist that the case has not been fairly represented to the minister by the officers of his department or he would more favourably consider the claims of Kinkora to a booking station. I stated last year that these men have to go to Emerald to receive their goods and have to drive 12 or 15 miles or else waste a day on the train. Then these trains often arrive at midnight. A booking station would not cost the government much as they have to keep a man there now. At the same time I might just as well urge the necessity of having two trains daily on that branch. There is only one train a day now and for the convenience of the travelling public and of the commercial people down there, there should be two trains. I am glad to find that the minister has decided to grant a station at Kensington and an extension to their siding. Fredericton. Breadalbane and Alberton are also to have new stations. I understand that the Alberton station is to be a flne brick station according to the minister's statement last year. I would ask whether it is proposed to abolish the nuisance of the ' Y ' that is used in order to get into Alberton station. This is a very inconvenient way of getting into the town, and for a reasonable expenditure it could be remedied. The abolition of the ' Y ' is just ns important to the operation of the railway as is the straightening of a good many of the curves.

I have given that matter considerable study personally ; I have also conferred with the officials, and T may say that this work would mean an expend!-

ture of probably $25,000. There is a similar ' Y ' on the Canadian Pacific Railway at Ottawa and they seem to get along very well notwithstanding. In my judgment, and in the judgment of the officials, the conditions prevailing at Alberton would-not justify such a large expenditure simply to avoid some little inconvenience in backing the trains.
What is the distance ?
About 3,000 feet. This matter has been pressed upon me by a great many friends but I could not concur in their conclusion. I hope to have the pleasure of visiting the island in the near future.
If the minister would come over and see the place I have no doubt he would change his mind.
Sherbrooke and Ottawa are in exactly the same position as respects the ' Y.'

That may be, but if Sherbrooke and Ottawa are content to remain in the slough, that is no reason why Prince Edward Island should not make progress. If the minister carried out these improvements on the island it would make him more popular.
Then you would feel bad.

Not at all. I am afraid that the people of Alberton have very little to hope for from the minister. The minister talks about an expenditure of $25,000, but that is a paltry sum to this government with their surpluses rolling in. If the Minister of Railways would whisper to the Finance Minister, he would tell him to go ahead, that it tvas only a drop in the bucket.
Then you would complain of the expenditure.

I am told by my colleague (Mr. Hackett) that the new stations at Northam and Richmond are going to be erected at once and I now remark that it is about time they should be. I again call the attention of the minister to the fact that the station accommodation at Summer-side is badly in need of improvement. The station is located just at the head of the railway wharf ; there is a considerable amount of traffic there every day, and serious accidents have occurred while others have been narrowly averted. This matter has been pressed upon the minister by the people of Summerside and by resolution of the Maritime Board of Trade, and I trust the hon. gentleman will give his attention to this matter immediately. I have many times brought to the attention of the House the construction of branch lines in Prince Edward Island, and I trust now to have the assistance of my hon. friend from King's * (Mr. J. ,T. Hughes) and my hon. friend from
Queen's (Mr. Haszard) in urging on the minister the necessity for railway extension. In Prince Edward Island there is only room for one system of railway, so that unfortunately we are debarred from the benefits which railway competition would give us. That being so the government should endeavour to meet the deficiency by affording adequate railway accommodation to the people. 'These branch lines have been promised to us more .than once and it is high time these promises were carried into effect. While the government has built the Murray Harbour branch for the people of that district, there are other localities on the island which are even more badly in need of railway communication. There is a branch badly needed from Westpoint to the main line. The facilities for shipping by water at West Point are not of the best, nor is it probable that a suitable harbour could be constructed there. The people have now no means of getting in their coal, and other supplies, or sending their products to the market. I hope the minister will see his w-ay to construct this branch line immediately. I have also brought to the attention of the House on many occasions the necessity of a branch line between Crapaud and North Wiltshire, and while I do not wish to elaborate on the arguments I have advanced on other occasions in favour of this undertaking ; I nevertheless earnestly press it upon the favourable consideration of the minister. During the by-election in Queen's, which resulted in fhe return of Mr. Haszard, there were strong resolutions passed in favour of a branch line from New London to a point on the main line of the Prince Edward Island Railway.
The necessity of a branch railway in that section of the island was very strongly- urged, and I understand that the hon. member for West Queen's (Mr. Haszard) gave his promise that if he were returned to parliament that branch would certainly be constructed. I hope the minister will give us his assurance to-night that that will be done. In order to fully round out the Prince Edward Island Railway and to put it in closer touch with the main line of the Intercolonial Railway, I would urge on the government the necessity of taking over the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island Railway, and making it the connecting link between the Prince Edward Island Railway and the Intercolonial. I believe the hon. Minister of Railways will see eye to eye with me as to the advantage this would be to both systems, and the added convenience it would be to the government in carrying out the terms of confederation with Prince Edward Island by providing a suitable service both winter and summer. I will not enter into any argument on this question to-night, but I submit it to the hon. Minister of Railways and his colleagues for careful consideration, and I believe

it will meet with their approval. Another matter connected with the railways, and allied very closely to them, is that of express accommodation between the western provinces and the eastern provinces. I understand that the Canadian Express Company has almost exclusive rights to a great many points on the Intercolonial Railway, while the Dominion Express Company is debarred from having access to those points. I know that the fruit growers of the west and the shippers of perishable products such as fish and meats in the maritime provinces, especially down about Canso, Halifax and other points not touched by the Dominion Express Company, are under a very serious disadvantage in getting their products to market. In many cases it is not possible to do so without the payment of a double ex-pressage. I have in my hand a letter from one of the shippers, which points out that resolutions were passed and forwarded to the Minister of Railways on this subject, and I would like to know from Mm later on in this debate what conclusion he has come to with regard to giving relief to the shippers in this matter. The following resolution was passed by the Board of Trade of Canso :
Whereas, the fish trade of Canso demands the very best transportation facilities possible, and whereas, the delays in the delivery of express shipments at present is one of the most serious obstacles to the building up of the business ; and whereas, wherever competition in express service exists a much better service is given ; therefore resolved, that we request the Minister of Railways to grant to the Dominion Express Company equal facilities and equal rights with the Canadian Express Company over all lines of the Intercolonial Railway.
This is a very serious matter, especially with regard to the shipment of fresh fish from the maritime provinces to western Canada : and speaking from my own experience. I think every facility should be given to the people of the maritime provinces to put a good article on the market, because there are no fish up here worth eating. The Council of the Halifax Board of Trade also passed a very strong resolution to the following effect and forwarded it to the Minister of Railways :
Whereas, the Dominion Express Company operates an express service on Intercolonial trains between St. John and Halifax affording competition to stations between these points ; and whereas, between Halifax and Sydney, and Truro and Sydney, the express service is confined to the Canadian Express Company, affording no competition to and from points reached by the Dominion Express Company on other lines of railway without two express charges being enacted ; and whereas, it is understood that the Dominion Express Company are willing to extend their service on all passenger trains of the Intercolonial Railway on same terms as are now grante 1 to the Canadian Express Company ; therefore resolved, that in thfe interest of im-Mr. LEFTTRGEY.
porters and shippers the council of the Halifax Board of Trade urges upon the Minister of Railways the advisability of granting the same terms to the Dominion Express Company as granted by the government to the Canadian Express Company ; and further resolved, that cbpies of this resolution he sent to the Minister of Railways, Finance and to the members for city and county of Halifax at Ottawa.
I would like to know from the minister that this matter has received his attention, and that he has some definite line of policy to announce to the House in regard to it.
Have you anything from Manitoba ?

The hon. gentleman is not possibly so much concerned for the interests of the maritime provinces as he might be. If we heard, his voice a little oftener upon certain subjects, for instance, the Elmira branch and some other matters, which he was loudly advocating when looking for votes in King's county, he would be much more appreciated. As 1 told him on one occasion, I am not here simply to represent my own constituency ; I consider myself as representing the Dominion of Canada at large ; and while the hon. gentleman does not see fit to look after his own constituency, I will have to point out ou the floor of this House certain needed improvements in that district. Coming back to the express companies, Prince Edward Island suffers from an added grievance in the fact that during the winter season all our express matter stops at Charlottetown, and we have to pay an extra amount to the Prince Edward Island Railway for its shipment to different parts of the island. That is certainly a great inconvenience to shippers.
Arrangements -with the railway could readily be made to give Georgetown, Souris, Summerside. Tignish. and Alberton express accommodation, and I would strongly urge on the minister the necessity of giving this increased accommodation to the importers in Prince Edward Island. Without trenching upon the matter of the conduct of the mails from the mainland, on which I shall have something to say on another occasion, I believe that there were twenty-eight days on which the mails came over, that Summer-side did not receive its foreign mail, and there were eighteen days on which these mails could have been forwarded to Summerside had the Department of Railways given the people a special train for their distribution, so that while the mails reached Charlottetown for distribution, they were held over there for many hours before they were forwarded to Summerside and points west, and on the other ten days the mails coming into the capes were sent to Charlottetown and brought back the following day. I have pointed out a great many of the grievances under which the people of Prince Edward Island are suffering in the matter of railway

and transportation facilities and also some on the mainland, and I think that if the hou. minister will take these seriously into his consideration, he will give better accommodation to the people of the different localities and the shippers and travelling public and wipe out a substantial part of the deficit which has been rolling up on the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island railways during the past season.

It is not my intention to follow the hon. gentleman from East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) in the long and somewhat rambling speech he has just delivered. The only conclusion I can draw from it is that he has abandoned the county of Prince and intends seeking election in Queen's county.
I have been offered the nomination down there.

No doubt he will find a few friends to encourage him, but if he accepts he will experience the same trouble there that he found himself in during the by-election as the electors did not pay much attention to him. The interests of the mussed mud diggers of his county are important, but had he stayed at home, when that industry was being carried on, in February last, and attended to the interests of his constituents, he might have met with more success. Instead of that he followed me through the riding of West Queen's and no doubt discovered that his chances for re-election in that part of the county were so slim that he is now looking for a nomination in Charlottetown. I do not believe in taking up the time of this House in airing our grievances and calling the attention of hon. gentlemen to them, who cannot be expected to be interested in these local matters. I appreciate the fact that much better and more effective work can be done by interviewing the proper ministers at the proper time, and I have no doubt that when the supplementary estimates are brought down I shall be able to convince the people of my riding that I have not been idle in attending to their requirements. The hon. gentleman also made some reference to the necessity of having a new station at Charlottetown-a question which has already been pretty fully threshed out. But his statement to-night does not agree at all with that of the hon. member'for Lincoln, who only a night or two ago said that the people of Charlottetown had no right to have anything to say regarding where that station should be built. I claim that the people should be consulted, and the question I think is now being dealt with in the only way that will be satisfactory to them. I shall not take up further time in following the hon. gentleman, but simply want him to understand that the people of Charlottetown and West Queen's have placed their confidence and trust in me. and if the hon. gentleman has no grievance to urge on behalf of Prince county, that speaks very well 199
for the government. They must certainly have been doing a good deal for that part of the island, since the hon. gentleman has confined his remarks almost altogether to the riding I have the honour to represent. No doubtriiowever, the speech which the hon. gentleman has delivered will be circulated broadcast throughout Canada, and possibly adorned by his photograph, as was the speech he made the other day.

The hon. gentleman who has just spoken has failed to appreciate the ideas advanced by this side. The proposition advanced by this side is not that the people of the locality shall not have a voice in determining where a station shall be located, but that the matter shall not be made a political engine by which to win votes. What we contend is that the administration ought to take the responsibility of coming to a decision and not leave these items in. the estimates dangling before the public from year to year for election purposes. I want to ask the hon. minister whether there has been anything done with reference to the purchase of the Canada Eastern Railway. That was discussed a good deal some time ago in the press. It was said that the government were negotiating for its purchase, and at the time when the minister was considerably engaged outside the House, it was supposed that he was engaged in these negotiations. It would be interesting to the public to know how far that matter has advanced.

I think what is of more interest at this moment is the item before the House. My hon. friend heard the announcement of the Prime Minister with respect to that matter, and if he will only possess his soul in patience he may learn something more about it.
I did not happen to hear the Prime Minister and I do not think It would be out of place for the hon. gentleman to inform the committee in what position that matter is now.

I think that my hon. friend is travelling outside the record. We are not dealing with the Canada Eastern but with the Prince Edward Island Railway. But as my hon. friend says he did not hear the Prime Minister, I shall be very happy to tell him what the Prime Minister said. The Prime Minister said that there would probably be legislation introduced in this parliament having reference to the Cajiada Eastern Railway.
Has the government purchased the Canada Eastern '!
That my hon. friend will probably learn in time.
This would be a good time to give the information.

The hon. member for East Prince (Sir. Lefurgey) seems to have



silently stolen away, but be made a number of statements and suggestions which call for some attention on my part. The first was as to the non-furnishing of sufficient cars on the Prince Edward Island Railway for the hauling of mussel mud. It was well known that the storms of last winter tvere very severe and impeded railway traffic in all parts of Canada. Prince Edward Island was no exception. For a time the railway was unable to carry on its traffic, and the shippers of mussel mud were not able to get cars as fast as they wished them or as fast as the railway would have liked to furnish them. But the difficulty was soon cleared away and the cars were supplied. He read a communication from the employees with reference to the pension scheme on the government railways. He received that communication in March last, and I am sorry he did not make it known to me. Almost all the members on this side received similar communlicajtions and thely made the matter known to me, and we have conferred with respect to it. Complaint is made with regard to the Boston travel. My bon. friend must know that during the past two seasons a special train has run between Point du Ch6ne and Boston, connecting with the train on the Boston and Maine. Cars come through from Boston to Point du Cheue, many of them ears of the Boston and Maine line. They are the same cars that are used on that line and on the Maine Central system, and are quite up to the standard of that system. It seems to me they should be fairly capable of meeting the requirements of the Intercolonial. This is a special train, and makes very quick time between Point du Chene and St. John and, in fact, right through to Boston.
Is it a mixed train ?

An express train. It connects with the Prince Edward Island Steam Navigation Company's steamer on her arrival and departure. The hon. gentleman also spoke of the line of railway along the harbour front in Charlottetown, and complained of the delays on the part of this government and of the Intercolonial manage ment. There is one very significant fact that he withheld from this committee. When he criticised this government and the present management of the Intercolonial on this point, he was certainly presenting a very severe indictment against my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart). When my hon. friend from South Lanark was Minister of Railways in 1888, if he was minister at that time-
No.

Then his predecessor in the Conservative government, which certainly was in power at that time-Mr. P S. Archibald, then engineer of the Intercolonial. was sent to Charlottetown and made a Mr. EMMERSON.
survey for a railway along the harbour front of that city. The year 1888 passed, and 1889, and so on up to and including 1896, during all of which time hon. gentlemen opposite were in power, and yet nothing was done. I do not know that my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) made any complaints against the government of that day with respect to their delay. This matter has received the attention of this government, and progress has been made. The proper connections are being made, and in due time the terminals at Charlottetown will be completed. Provision has been made in the estimates in connection with the station and the yards, and that is certainly more than the previous government did, though they led the people to believe that it would be done when they made that survey. The booking station to which the hon. gentleman refers would be at a place where the total freight earnings in the yard would not be enough to pay the expenses of maintaining the station. It would cost $700 a year to conduct, and the general manager advises me that there would not be that much of freight receipts in a year. It will be seen, therefore, that the officials on the Intercolonial are justified in reporting against it. But if circumstances later on justify it, we will establish it as a booking station. One of the hon. members cm the other side-I think it was my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster)-stated last night that we should rely upon the judgment of the officials of the road and not consult the wishes of the people. I had stated that the people of Charlottetown could not agree on a site for the station, and the hon. gentleman condemned me for consulting the people. That seems to be the new doctrine of hon. gentlemen apposite-or it may be their old doctrine. We are endeavouring to consult the wishes of the people and to meet their requirements in every possible way.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) was good enough to answer me with regard to the Canada Eastern. It would facilitate matters if he would state whether there is any foundation for the statement made in the newspapers the other day that the government was about to purchase the Canada Atlantic. Probably it would save time, and certainly would be more satisfactory to the committee in dealing with these estimates, if the hon. gentleman would tell us if that statement is well founded.

I was asked that question by one of the reporters last night, and I gave the answer. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) will look at the Toronto.
Globe ' of this morning-
Never read it.

I feared that. My hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) will remain in a benighted condition as long as he does not read the

Toronto ' Globe.' I made the statement last night, and I do not propose to enter into a discussion of that matter now. It would be entirely out of order. But I wish to be courteous to my hon. friend, and I will tell him where he can find the information.
Then the statement in the ' Globe ' is correct ?
Does the minister intend to take action this session with regard to a pension to the railway employees on the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railway ?

Perhaps my hon. friend did not hear me say that I hoped before the session was through to be able to introduce such a Bill. The premier stated from his place in the House the other day that such a Bill would probably be brought before parliament.
The hon. member for West Queen's (Mr. Haszard)'stated that the supplementary estimates were going to show something good for Prince Edward Island.
I have no doubt they will.
Would the minister state now what these supplementary estimates will contain ?
I have no idea what is in the mind of my hon. friend who made that statement, therefore I cannot answer for him.

Well it is difficult to get information on these matters respecting Prince Edward Island. There are two of ns here, my hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey). and myself, and we stand up for the rights of Prince Edward Island on every possible occasion where we think we can advance the interests of her people. Now the hon. member for King's, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes) this evening made what I consider a very unkind and very ungrateful remark. When my hon. friend from East Prince was speaking on matters affecting Prince Edward Island, the hon. member for King's interrupted him with the remark, What about Manitoba ? Are you going to advocate matters in connection with Manitoba ? Sir, it is too small. We are here representing Prince Edward Island, we are advocating the rights of Prince Edward Island, and when one of her representatives stands up here and advocates the rights of Prince Edward Island, he is told that he should also advocate matters in connection with Manitoba. I say it is unkind and ungrateful on the part of that hon. gentleman. Sir. the opportunity has arrived for the people of Prince Edward Island to be represented in matters affecting their interest, we wish to see justice done to our people in connection with railway stations and branch lines. Now the minister said that the Murray Harbour 1994
branch would be opened shortly. How is that progressing ? Is it intended to open it shortly ? How is the Hillsboro bridge getting along ? Will the Murray Harbour branch be open before the Hillsboro bridge is built ?

I want to say one word to my hon. friend who has referred to me. He says that I interrupted the hon. member for Erst Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) with a very unkind remark. That is not quite correct. The hon. member for East Prince was wandering in his speech all over the Dominion of Canada ; he was referring to Sydney, to Halifax and pretending that he had received communications from those ;cit.ie>s, that he had to discuss matters in relation to them. Certainly he was not then advocating the interests of Prince Edward Island, in fact, in my judgment, he was making himself-well, he was trying to spread out, and instead of advocating the interests of Prince Edward Island he was looking after other parts of Canada, and it was then that I interposed with the remark and asked if he had any communication from Manitoba.

After hearing the hon. member's explanation I repeat again that his interjection was unkind and ungrateful to the people of Prince Edward Island. My hon. friend from East Prince was advocating a better system on the Intercolonial, he was perfectly within his right in advocating an improvement of that system from Moncton to Halifax, he was justified in advocating that better accommodation should be given to the tourist travel over the main line of the Prince Edward Island Railway during the summer season. He complained that a change had been made at Painsec Junction, and that passengers travelling over the line had to change cars, and to go out of what might be called a fairly good palace car into an old dilapidated car that had been used for twenty years. The Minister of Railways said that was not so. I travelled myself over that line a little more than a month ago.- There is one car that goes to St. John, a Canadian Pacific Railway car I think it is.
No, it can't be that.

Then it must be a Boston and Maine car. There is only one car that goes through, and the passenger who has not been able to get a seat in that car must go out and hunt up another car to go down to Point du Chene.
When one car is filled up he has to get into another. Is that it ?
Yes. Now would you imagine in an up-to-date railway that all the travellers going down from Painsec Junction to Point du Chene have to change cars ?
They don't change at Painsec, the train goes right through.
Only one ear goes through.

But this season, during the summer travel, or the tourist travel as it is called, there is a special train known as the Boston train that goes right through from Boston to Point du Chene to connect with the island steamers, and it returns from Point du Chene right through to Boston. Some of the cars are Boston and Maine cars, others are Intercolonial cars. My hou. friend is certainly not well informed with respect to that matter, or he would not say that they have to change at Painsec. It is a through train, and is known as a special schedule train, it is on the time table of the Intercolonial and is known on the time table as the Boston train.
That change must have taken place very recently.
It is only during the summer season when the tourist traffic is on.
I had to change cars on May 15th.
Summer had not come then nor had the tourists.
It ought to be along on May 15th if we are to have any at all.
Last year there was the same improvement during the tourist season.

I want to resent the insult cast upon my hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) when he was advocating something in the interests of Prince Edward Island by the hon. member for King's (Mr. J. J. Hughes). The people of Prince Edward Island are all interested in having a large tourist travel and wTe want to have the best accommodation possible from Painsec Junction to Point du CMne, because we have as good boats between Point du Chene and Summerside as can be found in Canada or anywhere else, and therefore in order that we may keep up a good system of travel between the continent of America and Prince Edward Island it is necessary that we should have fairly good accommodation between Point du Chene and Painsec Junction. In regard to the station at Ivinkora, which is a good old Irish name, I may say that accommodation is required there for the factories, manufacturing all kinds of agricultural implements, and for the people of the surrounding district, which is one of the best farming portions of p.ur island, inhabited by a thrifty, hardy, intelligent people. Does the minister not think it necessary to build a station there which would provide the accommodation of a booking station ? I would appeal to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) who was in that Mr. EMMERSON.
province during a by-election some few years ago and who promised these people great things. He said : We are going to build a station ; you will have a booking station and all the facilities you require ; we will place you on the same footing as other parts of Prince Edward Island.
Hold him to it.
Will you do it now, may I ask the hon. Minister of Finance ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All the promises I made, if I made any, to the people of Prince Edward Island have been fulfilled long ago. I do not wait until this time to fulfil them.
What about the station?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Never, never, never; it is a dream of my hon. friend (Mr. Hackett).

It is a dream now, it is a dream of the past. You have forgotten all about what you promised to the people of Emerald and Kinkora in this connection. I met the minister at some of those meetings and he promised everything a minister could promise to obtain votes to elect his candidate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He got them, too.

As we are dealing with the total working expenses of the government railway system, it is perfectly right that the committee should be informed distinctly and explicitly as to whether the government proposes to purchase this Canada Eastern Railway, and the terms upon which the purchase is to be made. It wrould be only right and fair if he gave us full information in regard to the purchase of this railway, which I believe is owned by a gentleman in the House, a supporter of the present administration.

The statement was made by the Prime .Minister that this purchase was under consideration, and that the probabilities were that legislation to that effect would be brought down this session. I do not think it is fair to press the minister any further, in reference to this matter. For my own part, I only hope it is true that we are going to buy the Canada Eastern and I hope that this is only the commencement of the policy of purchasing all the feeders of the Intercolonial in the maritime province^. I am convinced that if the Grand Trunk Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway owned the Intercolonial, it would not be many months before they would acquire not only the Canada Eastern, but the other small railways, such as the Havelock Railway, the New Brunswick Railway previously spoken of. the Cumberland Railway and Coal Company, the lines of the Canada Coals and Railway Company and the other feeders to the Intercolonial Railway in the maritime provinces. I believe that this wise policy will be adopted in the future in reference

to these small railways In those provinces. Many of these railways are so conducted that the road-bed is not in proper shape, and many of the roads-although I do not now refer to the Cumberland Railway and Coal Company's lines-are not maintained in safe condition and accidents have happened which would not have happened if the government owned the railways and kept them up to the standard of the Intercolonial Railway.	.
i am firmly convinced that this is the proper policy'to adopt in reference to these feeders to the Intercolonial Railway. I did not intend to speak in the committee, but there seems to be a plan amongst hon. gentlemen on the other side to obstruct business, and I do not see why I should not have something to say as well as these gentlemen. We have had to-night a sample of the varied'views of the opposition upon the question of railway operation. The hon. member for East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) had the floor for more than an hour while he called upon the Minister of Railways to build in his district of Prince Edward Island. stations and sidings by the score, to make improvements without number, to run more trains, to build branch lines, and last but not least, to purchase the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island Railway. I tried to figure what would be the probable cost of carrying out his requests, and I find that it would amount to between $2,000,000 and $3,000,000. My hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) on the other hand, has referred to a large expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway as most reprehensible.
I have done nothing of the kind.
Well, it does not make much difference anyway what the hon. gentleman iMr. Lennox) said in reference to the matter.
It makes some difference that the hon. gentleman should misrepresent me.

I will not hesitate for a moment to take the hon. gentleman s woid, but I shall quote even a higher authority than he is on that question. I shall quote the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Haggart) who I have no doubt will be the Minister of Railways in the next Conservative government, whenever the time comes that a Conservative government is in powei.
Next election.
I am sorry to think that my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) will not live that long.

I regret that my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart) whom we all respect so much and whose genial niantiei we appreciate is not a younger man , because gray as his hair is now, it will be whiter than the driven snow before he has a chance to be Minister of Railways again. However, he was Minister of Railways once upon a time, and a few evenings ago in discussing the expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway, with tears in his eyes almost, and with a'tremor in his voice, he proclaimed :
Has the Minister of Railways no pity for the poor ratepayers of Canada ? .... Is the House going to submit to this ? .... Is the country going to submit to it ? ..	The
building of deep water termini and such thongs are interminable and are not justified at all ... . The Intercolonial Railway is a sink hole.
The hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Hag-o-artl denounced the building of sidings on the Intercolonial Railway, hut now the member for East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) demands sidings and improvements on the Prince Edward Island Railway which would cost millions of dollars. How can the people of Canada take the opposition seriously ? They are as much divided on this question as they are on the question of government ownership. I have no doubt that the speech of my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) was not intended for this House but for his constituents and I am convinced that that speech in pamphlet form will supply interesting reading by the firesides of East Prince m the cold winter evenings. Now, as to tne request with reference to the express companies ; I believe it is the general desire of the people living along the Intercolonial Railway that the Dominion Express Company should have the same privileges on that railway as are enjoyed by the Canadian Express Company. A number of us on tnis side of the House have recently waited upon the Minister of Railways in reference to this matter, and he has promised a sympathetic consideration, and expressed the hope that he will be able to look into the question within the next few weeks. I have no doubt the minister will come to the conclusion that the request of the Dominion Express Company 'should be granted. The hon. gentleman from East Prince (Mr Lefurgey) complained that there was a lack of cars'on the Prince Edward Island Railway. Iam sorry to say that there is also a ' lack of cars on the Intercolonial Railway, as I know from experience because 1 have just been endeavouring to secure cars for certain excursions which would not be objected to by my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes) or my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule). There is undoubtedly a lack of rolling stock on the government railways, but liow are we going to remedy that deficiency if attention is paid to the argument of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) who says that the Intercolonial Railway is a sink hole, and (that such expenditure is unjustifiable? We

need rolling stock, and a good deal of it.' and I hope tlie Minister of Railways will make provision to supply sucli rolling stock as is required. We have on the Intercolonial Railway some magnificent trains ; we have the best road-bed in the Dominion of Canada. but we have not sufficient passenger or freight cars. There is complaint from the shippers of the maritime provinces that they cannot secure facilities for the shipment of lumber and hay and other products. My hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) has referred to the tremendous crowds of people coming! from Boston to Prince Edward Island. I am glad to know that the exodus from Prince Edward Island has ceased and that the people are returning to that fertile province in such prosperous circumstances that they can afford to travel in parlour cars. But what has the hon. member for East Prince to complain of ? During the ten months of the last fiscal year ending on the! 1st of May, this government has spent the sum of -$364,924.66 chargeable to capital account on the Prince Edward Island Railway. What more does my hon. friend want? This government has spent on the Prince Edward Island road within the last few years over $2,000,000 on capital account. It would seem to me as if the government was doing its duty to the Prince Edward Island, Railway in this regard. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lefurgey) will only be patient he will find that the present government will amply supply the wants of the people of Prince Edward Island in the matter of railway accommodation.

Whenever the Minister of Railways is asked an important question I notice that some of his supporters pop up and endeavour to evade the issue raised. The Minister of Railways apparently has not the confidence of his supporters to such an extent that they will allow him to answer a question.
You were not present to hear the minister answer the question.
I have been here all day trying to hear him answer.
Where were you yesterday and the day before ?
I have been in this House as much as you have, and taken a greater part in the debates.
1 can say that that statement is absolutely and unqualifiedly a false statement.

If the hon. gentleman had the manners of any decent man he would not make that statement. It is only a man of his reputation who would do so. There was a question asked from the" Minister of Railways about the purchase of Mr. LOGAN.	[DOT]
the Canada Eastern Railway, and he has not answered it. There is a vote before this House for $7,000,000. and we are entitled to an answer "as to the policy of the government on that matter before we pass this item.

It is indeed refreshing to hear the voice of the hon. gentleman in this chamber once more. There is one thing about him, that when he does come in, which is a rare occurrence, he tries to make himself heard, and I congratulate him upon giving us his views on matters pertaining to the administration of the Intercolonial Railway. I desire, however, to point out that certain anomalies crop up from time to time in these discussions on the Intercolonial. I had intended to reply to certain matters brought up by the hon. member for East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey), who addressed the House at great length this evening ; but the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) having replied, it is not necessary for me to do so again. It was my intention to remind him that a communication was received by him in March last in regard to a matter of extreme importance to the employees of the Intercolonial Railway and the Prince Edward Island Railway. I intended to ask him before he concluded his observations wTkat action he had taken in regard to that communication. -Several members on this side of the House have received the same communication ; but they have not treated it as did the hon. member, who tonight professed such great anxiety for the interests of those people. They went to the minister in regard to the representations there made, they were received favourably by him, and I hope the impression they made on the minister will bear fruit that will be appreciated by the employees of the Intercolonial RailVay and Princ^ Edward Island Railway. If they had desired to use this matter for political purposes, it is probable that they would have kept these letters and resolutions in their pockets and waited three or four months to bring them up in the House and parade them before the people of this country to show that they were interested in those railway employees. They did not do that. They preferred to go about this matter in a businesslike way, and I have no doubt the employees of the Intercolonial Railway and the Prince Edward Island Railway will reap the benefits of the efforts those members on this side of the House have made in their interests. It is important that the people who have communicated with the hon. gentleman should know that * the communication which they sent him in March last has remained in his pocket, and that he has not brought it to the attention of either the minister or the country until after the lapse of four months. They will hardly thank him for his conduct in this matter. They will realize that it is not so much the interests of the people employed on

tlie Intercolonial Railway or the Prince Ed ward Island Railway that he desires to promote as it is his own interests.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman how long it is since he waited on the minister with regard to the railway employees ?

I want to say to my hon. friend and the committee that before this year, before that communication had been received, before the present Minister of Railways had assumed his present office, hon. members on this side of the House, together with myself, moved for a measure of this character, which I hope the Minister of Railways will submit to this House before the present session closes.

That is very unsatisfactory. My hon. friend from East Prince read a document here, signed in March last. Has the hon. gentleman waited on the hon. minister since ; and, if so, what effect has he had on the minister ?

I certainly have. Immediately on receipt of that communication I brought its subject matter to the attention of the minister, not for the first time, and again urged, upon him the desirability of passing such a measure in the interest of those people.

My hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey), from purely patriotic motives, in the interest of the employees of the railway, brought this matter before the attention of this committee this evening. Now, my hon. friend (Mr. Alex. Johnston) desires to reflect upon my hon. friend from East Prince, and to take the credit to himself. He said he had been working for a year or for two years. What success has he yet achieved in those two years ? The hon. member for East Prince had the manliness to come forward and present to this committee this document, signed by thc-different associations down there.
Where has the document been in the meantime ?

The original was before the minister. This is a copy that was sent to the hon. member for East Prince, and the hon. minister must also have had it before him. Why did the hon. gentleman not bring this matter before this parliament before ? Why did he wait for two years to have it brought up ? While my hon. friend from East Prince has been working in the interest of the railway employees, the hon. gentleman has remained as dumb as an oyster. I want to say one word in reply to the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan), who has also made an attack on the hon. member for East Prince. He says we require millions of dollars. We require no millions of dollars. This government undertook to build a branch line from Southport to Murray Harbour, which has cost $1,000,000 or 12,000,000. They also undertook to build a bridge. The accommodation required on the main line of the railway does not require millions. It would only take a few thousand dollars to grant this accommodation to the people. I made the remark a few minutes ago that when the Minister of Finance was down there he made great promises to the people of Prince Edward Island with regard to providing accommodation of this kind, but he has failed to carry out those promises. To come down to a later date, I find that the hon. gentleman last year made promises in parliament which he has not carried out. On an item for increased accommodation at Charlottetown, $87,000, we had the following discussion :
What work does this vote contemplate ?

'We are proposing to have a new station with covered platform, additional freight shed accommodation, additional land required for the purpose, re-arrangement of the yard, additional siding room, additional wharf accommodation, with dredging, and the usual allowance for engineering, inspection and advertising. The largest item is the new station and platform, $55,000 ; the next, the rearrangement of the yard, $11,000.
I ask the Minister of Finance, who was then administering the Railway Department, what has he done with regard to that Charlottetown station. Has he carried out that promise made last year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has spoken of some promise. I do not know of any. We took an appropriation to provide Charlottetown with a new station and we mean to do it. It could not very well have been done after parliament prorogued last October. My hon. friend can make his mind easy, Charlottetown will have a new station.

The people of Charlottetown are supposed to wait until doomsday for the accomplishment of these-promises. Year after year a certain amount has been appearing in the estimates for the purpose of building a railway station, and nothing is done. And the same statement which the Finance Minister made a mometvt ago is made every year. He was down there last autumn when it was supposed the elections were approaching. That was before the Grand Trunk Pacific difficulty. He must have looked over the site, and certainly can now whisper into the ear of his colleague that something should be done In connection with the building of this station.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will whisper.
Is the minister going to answer the question I put regarding the purchase of the Canada Eastern Railway ?

I did not think my hon. friend was serious. He knows that I am not privileged to declare the policy of the government. The Prime Minister is the one to make announcements of that kind. When the matter is in a condition to be brought before parliament, it will come up in the regular way.
I am not gifted with the power of humour which the hon. minister possesses.
No one would charge you with humour.

But in all seriousness I consider that parliament has a right to the information I have asked. We have got two rival policies before us. We have the policy propounded by the government of building the Grand Trunk Pacific and crippling the Intercolonial. On the other hand, we have the proposition involved in the question of whether this additional feeder shall be purchased to increase the usefulness of the Intercolonial. The question before us now is whether we shall or not devote a matter of some $7,000,000 to the maintain-ance of these roads.
$6,500,000, and we have passed that item. We are now over on the island and the Canada Eastern is not on the island.

We have not yet passed vote No. 250, which is one of $7,000,000, we are considering its various subdivisions. In considering the question whether we shall vote this money or not, we have the right to insist on being informed of the policy of the government. We have the right to know whether, notwithstanding the policy of building a transcontinental railway, which will necessarily cripple 'the Intercolonial, we shall adopt as a rival policy the extension of the principle of government ownership, by purchasing the Canada Eastern as a feeder for the Intercolonial. It is all important that we should know exactly where the government stand in this regard. We have the announcement of the First Minister that the principle of government ownership is to be extended by the purchase of this railway, because he informed us that there probably would be legislation brought down this year having reference to it. That could mean nothing else except legislation for the purpose of acquiring this road. Therefore the committee is entitled beyond question to this information at this time. We have to determine not only whether we shall devote $7,000,000 to the ordinary expenditure of the Intercolonial and the other road for the year ending 1905, but also that other question which is involved in it, and that is whether we shall connect the Intercolonial with this Canada Eastern, which it is said the government contemplate purchasing. The two things go Mr. LENNOX.
together, and it is time the House knew exactly what the government propose doing.
Has the Prince Edward branch sufficient rolling stock to meet its requirements ?
I am informed by the general manager that it would be very desirable to have some more.
There is not much satis-, faction in that answer. What class of cars is required ? What is the rolling stock that is deficient ?
There has been enough to meet the requirements. Business is increasing and as it increases we shall need more.
What is the number of cars ?
The total number is 446.
And the number of box cars is 213 ?
Yes.
What portion of these are in active service ?
All of them, except about five per cent that are usually undergoing repairs.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say that the failure in the train service on the Prince Edward Island Railway last winter was due to the snow blockade ?
That is what I was informed at the time, and I so informed my hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey). On receiving the complaint, I communicated with the officials, and that is the answer I got.
Will the hon. gentleman look over the train mileage of the road and tell us what was the mileage for August ?

And the snow blockade, I
suppose, took place about January or February ?

I think it-was during March.
. Mr. INGRAM. Will the hon. gentleman tell us what is the train mileage for March 1
It was 21,936.

Then, if business was the same, the falling off due to the snow blockade would be about as 25,000 to 21,000. Now, my hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) stated that there was an ' insufficiency in the train service all winter.
I am Informed by the general manager that the road has a larger number of trains in summer than in winter.

Then, that explanation makes the position of my hon. friend from East Prince all the stronger. It would show that the snow blockade affected the brain mileage very little or not at all. The minister has not thought this out. The excuse he makes is not in accordance with the figures he has given.

The statement I made was that the management reported to me, in answer to the complaint put in, that it was because of the snow blockade they could not furnish the cars, and I gave that answer at the time. The delay was only for a short time as I understand it. Soon after he made the complaint my hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) said that the matter was all right.
But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) made the statement that it was owing to the snow blftckade.
Because my officials told me so.
But the hon. gentleman is responsible for what his officials tell him
Certainly; I am taking the responsibility.

But surely the hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) will see the point. My hon. friend from East Prince said that the necessary train accommodation had not been furnished during the winter. The minister puts forward the excuse of the snow blockade. Any gentleman looking over the railways and canals report can satisfy himself that there was more snow in 1903 than in 1902. because in 1902 the snow ploughs were used for 2,330 miles, while in 1903 they were used for 14.020 miles. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) will see that this additional mileage was in March. If that be true

My hon. friend (Mr. Ingram can save himself a great deal of energy if he will recall the fact that this was during the month of March, 1904, and he is quoting the month of March, 1903. My hon. friend is quoting figures from the month of March, 1903. He is only a year out of the way.
The minister may be perfectly right, I have no doubt he is.
The hon. gentleman might save himself a good deal of fury.
How did it come to pass that the snow blockade in 1902 prevented the cars from being used in Prince Edward Island ?

I was speaking of the snow blockade this last winter. The complaint was made with respect to cars during March and February of this past year. But my hon. friend is quoting figures and returns for the year previous.

Now the hon. gentleman's snow blockade took place in the month of March. He could only say that in the month of March a snow blockade interfered with the cars and the trains. Now he explains that it was in January, February and April.

No, I did not say there was a snow blockade only in the month of March. We know that in Ontario and New
Brunswick, and other points there were snow blockades in February and January, and there may well have been in Prince Edward Island also.
If the snow blockade during the whole of the winter months prevented the train accommodation in Prince Edward Island being what the people required and desired

There was no complaint about the train accommodation of the island, or if there was a complaint, it came from a certain class of men who were hauling mussle mud to their farms. This last year they were a little late because of the deep snow, and they complained. But the general train service of the Island has not been complained of, that I have heard.
One of the representatives of Prince Edward Island has taken up nearly an hour in complaining of insufficient train service, and the hon. gentleman said that it was owing to the snow blockade.

No. As I understood the complaint of the hon. member Cor East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey), and as it was presented to me in communications wlncii L received, and about which I telegraphed in March last to the officials, it was merely from the mussel mud men who could not get enough cars. They wanted twenty-seven a day, I think it was, and they did not get that number in a week. The reason they did not get them in that week was the snow blockade, at least that is the reason assigned by the officials, they could not furnish the cars. I telegraphed to them, and immediately after that blockade was removed these men got all the cars they wanted.

My hon. friends were complaining about insufficient cars, the member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) also made a similar complaint. Let me mention that the revenue from the Prince Edward Island Railway for ten months was $189,894, and the expenditure during the same period was $255,056. The expenditure was more than $65,000 over the revenue. Now we find complaints about the insufficiency of cars, those who desired to ship could not secure cars in order to increase the revenue of that road. I tried to find out from the hon. gentleman if they had sufficient rolling stock to meet the requirements, and he has not explained to this House satisfactorily whether they have or not. He says they could put up with

more. Surely if the road is losing $05,000 in ten months owing to a shortage of cars, then it is necessary to have more cars to meet the requirements of trade. The hon. gentleman has not given us a satisfactory explanation with respect to that. Now the hon. member for Cumberland rose to answer some questions, and so did the hon. member for Cape Breton. I understand that some of these gentlemen, and this is not the first time, have interfered with that road. I understand some of these gentlemen go so far as to say that they must have trains to meet their convenience, and they simply give orders to the station agents : You must hold these trains till I am ready to go. X understand that has been done, and when one of the station agents refused to interfere with the progress of the trains, he was removed.
Will the hon. gentleman give the names ?
Yes, I will give the hon. gentleman a name privately, it is a member of this House.
I would like my hon. friend to be kind enough to give the name now.	,
I will give it privately.

It is not fair to hon. members of this House for the hon. gentleman to make that statement without giving names. The statement is made publicly, and it is but fair to give the name of the offender and of the official who was dismissed. I think it is due to the management that their names should be reported. 1 am sure that the hon. gentleman has been misinformed.
I hope so.

I am satisfied that he has been, and I will make this statement, challenging successful contradiction' that there never has been an official dismissed from the railway becausq he refused to detain a train at the request of a member of parliament or of anybody else.
Will the hon. gentleman go so far as to say that a station agent was not removed for refusing to comply with the request of a member of parliament ?

I will go so far as to deny that, if any request to detain a train was made by a member of parliament, the station agent was dismissed because he refused to detain the train. Now it is due to the department
I did not say that, you are not going to put words down my throat.
If my hon. friend wishes to withdraw

I withdraw nothing, I am not here to withdraw anything I have said. What I did say was that it was reported to Mr. INGRAM.
me that a certain member of this House went to a station agent and asked him to detain a train to suit his convenience. The train was not detained by the agent and by reason of the train not being detained, the agent was removed from that station.
I give that a most unqualified contradiction.
Very well ; I am very glad to hear that.

Nothing of the kind ever occurred. I think my hon. friend should in fairness to the hon. members from the maritime provinces give the name of his informant, the name of the member, the name of the station agent and the particular station. I think that information is due in all fairness.	.
I told the hon. gentleman that I would give^him the name privately.
We want it publicly.
I will do as I like about that.

I think that in fairness the name should be given. A stigma is placed on some one member of this House. That member should be known and if the charge is not true he should have an opportunity of giving it a contradiction, otherwise all the members from the maritime provinces are under that stigma.

The member whose name I have is a good respectable member of this House, and I have no desire to do him injury. I will tell the minister the name privately, and if I do him any injury by this statement I am man enough to stand up in the House and say it is not true. Is that fair ?
I think that in all fairness he should give the name.

I am the best judge of what I should do in this matter. I give you the complaint and if the complaint is not correct I will be as glad to hear it as the hon. minister, but if it is correct the sooner a matter of that kind is investigated and stopped the better.

If the hon. gentleman will give the name an investigation will be held and the true facts elicited. I-wish to say that no station agent has ever beeD dismissed on the Intercolonial Railway because

Mr. COCHRANE, tion to another.

the train at the request of a member of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It seems to be a rumour which we can get no one to father, and that is a poor rumour.
Does the minister approve of naming a member.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not approve of a gentleman taking an idle rumour of that character and flinging it before parliament when he has no authority and no one to back it up.
I have as good reason to state that as the hon. minister has to state what he said.	>

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not stated anything.
It would be more becoming the hon. gentleman not to say anything. What are we here for ?
That is a question.
That is a question.
To vote blindly.

If there is any statement in the public press of this country in connection with the management of any government institution and that comes under the eye of a member, parliament is the place where that member is supposed to state it, and if it is not correct it is neither belittling nor unbecoming to a minister to give an answer.
