speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has no father at all.
An idle rumour which has been set afloat which the hon. gentleman cannot connect with anybody.

Hon. gentlemen opposite, on the eve of a possible election, evidently do not want information as to the affairs of the country to be given to the people in answer to the questions which the people can only get through the opposition who are particularly charged with asking for information as to the administration of the country. I can quite understand that. They do not desire to have any clear announcement. The hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) has pointed out very calmly and earnestly in the discharge of his duty the importance of knowing whether the Canada Eastern, running from Fredericton to Chatham, is to be acquired by the government and made part of the Intercolonial. We are asked to pass an estimate of $7,000,000 for the maintenance of this railway,' and surely we are entitled to ask as to the acquisition of this Canada Eastern. The Minister of Railways perhaps does not know or care. He may be satisfied to get his estimates voted blindly, without giving any information on the subject whatever, and then use the estimate as he pleases-as he did with $4,000 which was voted for the acquisition of a station site. I understand that the Minister of Railways does not want to give us the information but we are obliged to tell him that we are entitled to it and that we must insist on having it.

The hon. gentleman is not justified in saying that I want to withhold the information. The question had reference to the policy of the government, and 1 said that the Prime Minister was the proper person to speak with regard to that. 1 do not feel that I would be at liberty to state what may be transpiring before council with respect to this or any other matter until it has reached a stage that it call be announced to parliament. The Prime Minister is the person to do that, or to delegate it especially to some of his colleagues. That is my position in the matter.
Did it occur to the Minister of Railway's that the Prime Minister should tell him not to try to get these estimates through until he was ready to give us information.

The only connection that question would have with the item under discussion is that should the government acquire this branch railway, it would involve further expenditure.
Mr. LANCASTER, That is not the only one.

If it should happen before the sessiqn closes that the government would ask parliament to acquire the Canada Eastern, the government would also have to ask parliament to vote money to maintain the Canada Eastern, and then would be the proper time to discuss
COMMON?
the matter, and the committee would have ample opportunity for discussion. No one desires to be discourteous to the opposition, but it is unreasonable to take the attitude that no estimate will be voted until the committee is informed as to the policy of the government regarding the Canada Eastern.
I did not say that.
That seems to me to be the attitude taken.

That is not my attitude.
Sir WILLIAM MULOCIv. Is it reasonable for the opposition to dwell further upon the refusal of the Minister of Railways to anticipate the Prime Minister's announcement, should the government decide that an announcement may be made with regard to this matter ? If the opposition were curtailed in their rights in any way I would be the first to resent it; but they are not in the slightest degree prejudiced by postponing the discussion on a matter which is not before the House, and which may never occur ; it may and it may not occur.

If the opposition choose to say that they are not going to allow these estimates to pass until the policy of the government respecting the Canada Eastern is announced, we come to a deadlock, and it becomes a question of physical endurance. Is that a desirable state of affairs ? It is quite as competent for the government to enter into a battle of that kind as it is for the opposition. I have been many years here and I have taken part in such contests, but I must say that I fail to discover wherein the public interest was advanced by any such method. I am sure that all will agree that nothing is to be gained tonight by the opposition adhering to the view that no progress will be made.
No one has suggested that.

I gathered that from the language of my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster). Is it fair to create an impasse because the Minister of Railways will not make an announcement that he is not at liberty to make ? If any announcement is to be made it will be made by the head of the government, or by some person properly authorized. There is no person authorized to make such an announcement to-night; vet hon. gentlemen opposite, in anticipation of something that may or may not happen, make that a causS for obstructing the passage of these estimates. I do not think that is reasonable.

Weeks ago it was announced in the government press that this Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
railway is to be purchased and made a part of the Intercolonial Railway. The question was asked of the Minister of Railways an hour ago, who saw fit to treat it in a somewhat supercilious manner.
Oh, no.
We have our own opinion about tha t.
I did not intend to.

Then the hon. gentleman's manner is unfortunate The government could have done one of three things when the question was put ; they could say: No, it is not to be purchased ; or, yes, it is to be purchased ; or they could say that the matter is under consideration. Any of these three answers might be given without any detriment to any public interest, and any one of these answers would be absolutely satisfactory.
If that is the question I can answer it at once.
That is practically the question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question before the committee is a vote for the Prince Edward Island Railway, and a question entirely foreign to that is being discussed. - Information is asked of the minister with regard to another railway which is not now under discussion. That is out of order, and I would not allow the minister to answer the question if he proposed to do so.

BORDEN-I move that the committee rise, and I ask whether or not there are any proposals under consideration, and whether or not the Canada Eastern Railway is to be purchased by the government 1 I may say that I do not agree with the ruling of the chairman, but it is not worth while wasting time over that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When a motion is made that the committee rise the discussion must be confined to giving reasons why the committee should rise.
The question that is to be considered on a motion that the committee rise is that which is introduced by the person who makes the motion

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Not at all.
Surely you should let the hon. gentleman malae his statement without rising up in the middle to interrupt him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I want to put myself right. The hon. gentleman has taken exception to my ruling, and it is my business to sustain my ruling. A motion that the committee rise is equivalent to a motion for the adjournment of the House. If such a motion is made during the dis-

eussion of a question, then the discussion must be confined to the question. But if a motion of adjournment is made in the House between the Orders of the Day, you can introduce any question you wish to discuss. The discussion on this motion must be confined to the question before the committee.

I would like to say to the Minister of Railways, after this luminous exposition by the Chairman that I do not regard it as sufficient for him to say that the Prime Minister is not here. We lduow that he must necessarily be absent sometimes during the sittings of the House, and we are ready to make every reasonable allowance ; but that is no reason why an item should be passed in his absence. The proper course would be to postpone the consideration of the item until the Prime Minister finds it convenient to be present. If questions arise as to which he only can speak during the discussion of an item, then he should appoint some one to speak for him in his absence, or the consideration of the item should be postponed until he has an oportunity to be present. However, I understood the Minister of Railways to say that there is no difficulty in answering the question.

The question first put to me was a comprehensive question, on which I was to give all the transaction, all that has transpired. If the question is as put by my hon. friend, whether the purchase of the Canada Eastern is under the consideration of the government, I would at once say yes.

That was not just the way I put it. I said that a question had been put to which I thought there could be one of three proper answers which ought to be satisfactory to the opposition. Has the Canada Eastern been purchased or is it about to be purchased by the government ? I thought the government might very well say that it has been purchased, or that it is about to be purchased, or that it is not to *be acquired, or that the matter is under consideration. Either of these answers would be fair.
The matter is under consideration.
That is to say it has not been decided.

As the minister says, the question, was somewhat comprehensive The first question I asked was : Has the railway been purchased ? I also asked : Is the government about to purchase it ? If so. we would like to have the particulars. The minister could have answered the question bv saying that they had not purchased it, but that the matter was under consideration. I understand the minister to say that they are about to purchase it and that the matter is under consideration.
Is that the answer of the hon. minister ?

Does it not follow that when the minister says the matter is under consideration, it may be that negotiations with the idea of purchase have been undertaken ; but you could not say that the matter had been completed, that a bargain had been agreed to, unless the details had been agreed upon. When you say it is under consideration, that is I think as liberal a statement as an opposition might reasonably expect.
I think we all understand the situation. The hon. Postmaster General is hedging a little for the benefit of the Minister of Railways and Canals.
The answer, I understand. is that the railway has actually been purchased, but the Minister of Railways and Canals does not choose to make that declaration.
I suppose that on your ruling, if the Minister of Railways had stated that the railway had been purchased, the question could not be considered at all under the item ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No, he would not be at all in order in answering. It has nothing to do with the question under discussion.

I wish to ask a few questions of the minister. According to his statement for the ten months ending the 30th of June last, there has been a deficit of about $65,005 iu receipts as compared with the expenditure and working expenses. Is there any anticipation that that deficit will cease ? The expenditure on capital account for the same period he states to be $346,000 ; yet the hon. minister retains $650,000 to his credit. Does he expect to use up during the unexpired two months the difference between those two amounts ?
About $300,000 of that would be expended during the two months.
About $300,000 more than the $343.(500. That would be $643,000 on capital account ?
That would mean for the whole twelve months.
What is the amount contemplated to be expended on capital account, after the vote of this year, on the Prince Edward Island Railway ?
On the Murray Harbour branch ?
Yes, and the other improvements. Does the vote of this year cover the whole expenditure contemplated on that branch ?
No, I gave the explanation and the information will be found in ' Hansard.' X move that the committee rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again.

I understand that tfie lion, minister will have in the supplementary estimates an item for the completion df work on the double track between Windsor Junction and Halifax. Last year the Minister of Finance, as- acting Minister of Railways, took an appropriation of $118,000, telling us at the time that that would not complete the work, and I understand that the minister will have to ask a further amount in the supplementaries. I presume that is so.
It will be necessary to have a further vote.

My object in asking that question now is this. When that item comes up on the supplementary estimates, I desire that the minister shall be ready to furnish us with all particulars about the work-the plans, profiles, specifications and contracts entered into, if any, and the tenders and everything concerning the work, so that we may be able to discuss it without asking further adjournment.
Some resolutions reported.
